In 1983 , the Rhode Island Department of Transportation ( RIDOT ) began construction of the new segment of Route 4 between exit

10 and exit 12. The new four-lane roadway was designed with a curvilinear roadway profile, a range of 21 percent to 33 percent, and a minimum horizontal curve radius of 1,600 feet. The project also included a new interchange at exit 10, which was located in Tiverton, and a new interchange at exit 12, which was located in Portsmouth.
 While RIDOT did not estimate the probable maximum flood ( PMF ) at the time the design was prepared, the state agency determined that the project would be subject to the PMF . The design specifications for the roadway included the following statement:
    "The design is based on a 100-year storm event which may occur once in
    100 years or less. The design is based on the assumption that there will
    be no flooding beyond the limits of the right of way."
The final design, which is included in the appendix to this decision, shows that the roadway is located 250 feet above sea level and that the adjacent creek, Mill Creek, is 50 feet above sea level. The project included a drainage system that, according to the RIDOT design specifications, "will be designed to drain the roadway during the 100-year flood."[1]
 RIDOT began construction of the Route 4 project in the summer of 1983. During the summer of 1986, the town of Tiverton adopted a zoning ordinance that created the 100-year flood plain for the Mill Creek watershed as a designated flood plain. The ordinance also created a "Flood Hazard Area" overlay district within the designated flood plain that was subject to various restrictions and limitations.[2] Tiverton sought to adopt the ordinance after the state Legislature enacted the Flood Hazard Zone Act in 1981 and after the state Executive Office of Environmental Management ( EOM ) had sought to enforce the Act by requiring the town to adopt the ordinance.[3] After a public hearing on the Tiverton ordinance, the town's zoning board of adjustment approved the ordinance on October 16, 1986, and the town council approved the ordinance on October 21, 1986. The ordinance became effective on November 17, 1986.
 In the spring of 1987, after the construction of the roadway was substantially completed, a large flood occurred in the Mill Creek watershed. The flood caused the roadway to be inundated with approximately 5 feet of water and caused the Mill Creek to overflow its banks. Mill Creek flooded the roadway along its entire length and submerged the roadbed, which was situated 250 feet above sea level, with approximately 5 feet of water. The flood destroyed the drainage system that had been built into the road, and the roadway was subsequently submerged by the flood water for three months. The flooding and the resulting damage to the roadway occurred because the roadway and its drainage system were not designed to pass water from Mill Creek during a flood.[4]
 On June 3, 1988, the town of Tiverton filed a complaint with this Commission against RIDOT asserting that the flooding of the roadway was caused by RIDOT 's failure to design the roadway to pass water from Mill Creek during a flood and by RIDOT 's failure to adequately maintain the roadway after it was constructed. The town seeks damages of $69,568.60 for the costs of repairing the roadway.
 The town petitioned this Commission for an order requiring RIDOT to repair the roadway and reimbursing the town for its costs of repair. The town also sought a declaratory judgment that the Commission has jurisdiction over the roadway under the Flood Hazard Zone Act. RIDOT petitioned the Commission to dismiss the town's complaint on the basis that the Commission does not have jurisdiction over the roadway because "[t]he roadway was constructed in compliance with the applicable standards and guidelines and was designed by persons possessing the appropriate qualifications."[5]

Stay @-@ at @-@ home dads make up a very small portion of the Australian population although this appears to be rapidly changin

g. The problem is that we are not well represented in our national statistics. This is because we are not collecting the data. As a result there are no figures available to show the extent of our demographic in comparison to the rest of the country. However, it appears that the number of workin g, stay at home dads is increasing. In the 1996 census there were 3. 5 million households with one working adult. 47% of these households were the sole breadwinners and of these 12. 4% were women. The other 52% of the households with one working adult included both a man and a woman.
The majority of these families were in the high income bracket. There was a considerable shift in the percentage of households with one working adult from 19% in 1986 to 47% in 1996. This is largely due to the growth of single parent families. The proportion of single parent families with the main earner being the mother has increased from 14% in 1986 to 32% in 1996. The proportion of single parent families with the father as the main earner has not changed significantly. The majority of the increase in single parent families is due to the divorce rate. This has increased from 19% in 1986 to 30% in 1996. In 1986 there were 39% more divorces than marriages and in 1996 the ratio had risen to 60% more divorces than marriages.
Divorce rates for women are considerably higher than for men. In 1975, 50% of the divorced men in Australia were still with their children, by 1986 the figure was down to 50% and by 1996 was only 40%. A major reason for this is the fact that the women have a harder time than the men in finding another job, especially if they are in their early 30s. However, in 1996 80% of the women who were divorced said they were in the labour force, working as a secondary earner to their children. This is changing as more and more women are working as their main income earner.
The increase in the divorce rate has also had an effect on the single parent families with the main income earner being the father. In 1975 50% of single parent families with the main income earner being the father had both biological parents. By 1986 the figure had dropped to 43% and it was only 38% in 1996. This is largely because of the fact that the father has a much harder time finding work. The majority of families with the father as the sole breadwinner are in the lower income bracket. The proportion of households with the mother as the sole breadwinner has increased from 5% in 1986 to 12% in 1996. The majority of these families are in the lower income brackets but there are some in the high income bracket. 48% of all single parent families with the main income earner being the mother are in the lower income bracket and 42% are in the middle or upper income bracket.

Instead, the Church teaches that sexual activity between persons who are in a relationship and who are not married is "gravely contrary to the moral law" if it is done with the intention of continuing the relationship. For example, two people may have a relationship that is so strong that it is a good in itself, even if they are not married, and they may engage in sexual activity without sin.  However, the Church also teaches that sexual activity between people who are not married is wrong, even if it is not sinful, because it is against the law of God.

It has been estimated that average @-@ sized bacteria contain about 2 million proteins per cell ( e.g. E. coli and Staphylococc

usaureus). These proteins may be involved in virtually every physiological function and it is likely that combinations of proteins may be responsible for many of these functions. It is also known that the bacterial cell surface membrane contains a variety of proteins that are involved in intercellular communication and signal transduction. It is also likely that the surface membrane contains a variety of receptors for carbohydrates, nucleic acids, lipids, and other proteins, and that the processes of protein transport and processing are intimately involved with these interactions. It is clear that many of the functions of the bacteria involve the interaction of proteins and membranes, and that these processes are mediated by proteins. Hence, the primary goal of the proposed research is to identify the proteins of the surface membrane of the bacteria and to determine their functions. The protein data bank at Brookhaven National Laboratory has been used to determine homology of the surface membrane proteins with other prokaryotic and eukaryotic proteins. The human B subunit of cholera toxin (CTB) and cholera toxin (CT) are used as model toxins that undergo receptor mediated endocytosis. The B subunit of CTB is a single chain protein of 28 kDa and is a receptor for CTB, whereas CT is a dimer of two identical 64 kDa subunits that are joined by a disulfide bond. Both subunits bind specifically to the surface membrane glycoprotein GM1 ganglioside and cause endocytosis of the toxin and its receptor into the bacterium. CTB has been shown to be an efficient immunogen and to protect against the toxin in animal models of diarrhea. A variety of mutant forms of CTB have been made to alter the protein in ways that affect the ability of the B subunit to bind CT or bind GM1 ganglioside. lefts " in the mountains of Ephraim and Benjamin, and the name was then given to the place. Jifna was at one time the capital of the district of Nablus . On the west it was bounded by the Jezreel Valley , on the north by the hilly country of Afula and Shefaram, on the east by the plain of the Jordan, and on the south by the valley of the Sorek. It was reached from Nablus by a road that ran over the mountain ridge of Latrun and north-east of the village and on the opposite side of the valley of Ain Karim, the Russian monastery of St. George was built, and from an elevation of 2500 feet the whole of the Shefaram valley can be seen. The village of Jifna lies on the top of a spur, the largest and highest elevation in the valley, and is about 1600 feet above the level of the sea. It is a small place, with about 500 inhabitants, and has two mosques and a school. It is surrounded by fertile and well-watered fields, and is pleasantly situated in the midst of olive groves and fruit trees. The mountain on which it is situated is a smooth curve, and from its summit, whence begins the wady Jiftlik, or Jifna, the whole of the valley can be seen. The bed of the wady is filled with loose stones, and the stream flows over them with great rapidity, and is often in spate, so that the villagers must pass over it in boats with their flocks during the rainy season. The wady ends in a small lake , called the Dephna , or " fountain," which is dry except during the winter months, when it is full of fish. From the lake the road turns up the valley, and crosses a deep ravine, called El Ka'ib, to reach the village of Beit Jibrin. The road from Nablus, which follows the course of the wady, is for the most part stony and difficult, but it is very picturesque, and is traversed by a number of ancient tombs, which are supposed to date back to the time of the Judges. The village of Jifna is, however, much less ancient, and it is probable that it was originally a fortified position, as it rises from the plain and is surrounded by hills. The present village is of very recent origin, and its present inhabitants are descendants of the Arabs who settled here during the Crusades. They are mostly poor, as the soil is very barren, though it is watered by innumerable springs. They are, however, very industrious and hard-working. Their chief occupation is the making of soap, as the village is considered one of the best for soap-making in Palestine. Some of the inhabitants are employed in the cultivation of the land, and others are gardeners. The chief natural products of the place are olives, figs and grapes, but of these the latter are the most valuable. The grapes are used mainly in the preparation of wine and vinegar, while the olives yield both oil and soap. In the village there are two mosques, one of which is very pretty, and is surrounded by a fine garden of olives. The inhabitants congregate in a large mosque, which is used also for the purpose of a school, and reading room. The village of Jifna is now nearly surrounded by the villages of Beit Jibrin and Beit 'Amra, which have grown up in the last thirty years. The force remained in Somalia until 25 March 1995, when the government of Somalia collapsed and the United Nations departed. The Temple of Eshmun ( Arabic : معبد أشمون ) is an ancient place of worship dedicated to Eshmun , the Phoenician god of healing

. It is located in the city of Sidon in modern-day Lebanon.
The archaeological site consists of a series of temples built over the course of more than a millennium, from the 10th to 6th centuries BCE. It was one of the earliest examples of the "temple-as-court" model adopted in the Levant by Phoenician cities such as Sidon. The area was under the control of the Phoenician city-state of Tyre until the 6th century BCE, when it became part of the Achaemenid Empire and then, in the 4th century, became a Greek city. The site was over time incorporated into the Church of St. Peter. In 1964, it was declared a National Monuments of Lebanon.

  1. Bath and North East Somerset ( / ˈ b æ θ æ n / ) is a unitary authority in the ceremonial county of Somerset , England . It is the largest local authority in the county. The main town is Bath , and the district that includes it was formerly known as Bath and North East Somerset . It has a population of 184,000 , a higher proportion of educated professionals than most other local authorities in England, and is the wealthiest local authority in England. The district is home to many of the country's largest employers, including the BBC , B&Q , Braun , Cadbury , the Co-op , the Royal United Hospitals Bath NHS Foundation Trust , the South West Regional Development Agency , the Wessex Water Authority , and the Wiltshire and North Somerset Air Ambulance . The district was created in 1996 from the former districts of Bath and North East Somerset and the non-metropolitan county authorities of North Somerset and the remainder of Somerset . In 2019, it was ranked as the second most effective local authority in the country by the Local Government Association . In 2010, 7.9% of the marriages registered in Bath and North East Somerset were same-sex marriages, compared with 6.4% in Brighton and Hove and 4.5% in Camden . In 2011, 8.2% of the marriages registered in Bath and North East Somerset were same-sex marriages, compared with 6.4% in Brighton and Hove and 4.3% in Camden . Geography Geology Bath and North East Somerset is an area of high natural and historic beauty. It is in the Avon Valley , and is a part of the Cotswold Hills . The rocks of the Cotswolds are a series of Mesozoic limestone and sandstone rocks. The limestone rocks are generally softer, and have been carved into the Cotswold scenery by the weather and by the work of people. These rocks are superficially weathered into a softer material called 'millstone grit ' . The Cotswolds area is the only outcrop of Triassic sandstone in England. The ground surface is dominated by Carboniferous limestone forming the limestone escarpments , and the Triassic sandstone and mudstone forming the plateau . The area is rich in natural beauty. It includes the countryside and the urban areas of the cities of Bath and Bristol . The Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary are in the area, and the whole area is within the Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary Biosphere Reserve . The largest lake in Bath and North East Somerset is Chew Valley Lake , a reservoir on the River Chew . The area has some of the most extensive areas of chalk grassland in Europe. The area is also in the Bristol Avon Corridor Special Area of Conservation and Ramsar site . More than 50 species of reptile have been recorded in the district, including six species of reptile listed as nationally scarce , as well as the nationally scarce water vole . The town's population grew rapidly, and the area around Oldham became a byword for hard work and industrial poverty. By the 1920s, Oldham faced extreme unemployment, poverty, and social deprivation. Its population had dropped by a half, and 1 in 4 people were unemployed.  In 1916, the Ordnance Survey map shows the town centre to be dominated by a network of streets, and with 4 thoroughfares and 3 main roads leading outwards. Oldham's cotton mills were built in the 1830s and 1840s, as the industry rapidly increased in scale and productivity. The town's population was mostly made up of mill workers.  Oldham's prosperity depended on its cotton mills. In the 1770s , the French naturalist Comte de Buffon stated that the dodo inhabited both Mauritius and Réunion . It is unclear

whether or not he actually saw the bird on Réunion; there are some references to him having seen a specimen taken from there , but  others  say that he saw one taken to France.  It is thought that he did see one preserved in Paris at the time, possibly at the Jardin des Plantes, but it is unlikely that he would have seen an alive dodo on Réunion, as there were only about 50 of them left alive in 1681,  and they became extinct in 1688.  The dodo was not seen on Réunion since the 1700s.  A specimen of the dodo was brought to Paris as a curio in 1705, but by then, the species was extinct on the island.  Some doubt has been cast on the authenticity of this specimen, but it was exhibited at the Jardin des Plantes in 1770, and is mentioned in the Jardin des Plantes' catalogue of 1778, which established that it was at least the skin of a dodo, and possibly the skin of a live bird.  The specimen was eventually lost in a fire in 1786.  The Jardin des Plantes also had a stuffed dodo in its collection , but its authenticity was doubted, and it was eventually lost in a fire in 1795.  Finally , in 1801, the Jardin des Plantes acquired the skin of a dodo from the Parisian merchant Pierre Sonnerat, and subsequently the dodo was included in the species list of the Jardin des Plantes.
 In 1982, a part of the skin of a dodo was rediscovered in the Arpmuseum of Dierenpark Amersfoort, Netherlands, under the name "Amersfoort dodo", which was described as a new species.  This was the first time that a dodo specimen could be reliably identified, and it was subsequently determined that it was a previously unknown specimen from Réunion.  This specimen was rediscovered in 1989 by the Dutch Reunion animal collector Jan Vos.  In 2002, the skin was restored to its original shape using a 3D reconstruction of the bone.  The skin contains 42 feathers, 25 of which were original to the dodo, and 17 of which were from birds that were added by a previous owner.

The creek is a tributary of the San Francisco Bay (it empties into the bay at the mouth of the Bayshore Freeway , between the Bayshore Freeway and the San Francisco Bay Trail ).
The creek was named after a former Dutch Burgher, Hendrik Van Du Vrees, who settled in the area in the 1770s.
The creek was originally a natural stream, but was filled in to make way for the 1906 Panama-Pacific International Exposition . Later, additional land was filled in from the creekbed to make way for the Bayshore Freeway, which cut off the creek from its natural watershed .
The creekbed is now maintained as a landscaped park called Islais Creek Park . The park is a part of the City of San Francisco's reclamation of the San Francisco Bay. The park also contains an open-air amphitheater and a small playground.
Islais Creek has a number of wildlife habitats. The area is home to a large number of shore birds and water fowl, including ducks, geese, and swans. These birds are attracted to the park by the man-made bodies of water. Shorebirds have been known to nest in the park. Islais Creek Park is one of the most important shorebird habitat in San Francisco and the surrounding area.

The Early Neolithic people of Britain placed far greater emphasis on the ritualised burial of the dead than their Mesolithic fo

reshadows. Some of these burials, mostly in the form of cremations, appear to have been accompanied by the use of special, decorated vessels. The earliest of these, the so-called Beaker People, lived in the Neolithic, while a second group, called the Bell Beakers, lived in the Early Bronze Age. A third, less well-documented group, have been termed the Boat Burial People, on account of their apparent association with burial in boats or boats-like vessels. The Boat Burial People are thought to have lived during the Middle and Late Bronze Age, but some scholars have suggested that they were already extinct by the end of the Early Bronze Age, and that the Boat Burial People were merely the last remnant of the Bell Beaker people. Others argue that the Boat Burial People were in fact the forefathers of the more widely distributed Bronze Age Bell Beakers, and that the latter were merely a subset of the former. However, the concept of a single, widely distributed group of Bronze Age people, who were closely related to but distinct from the Beaker People of the Neolithic, is a controversial one, and there is as yet no consensus among scholars on the matter. Nevertheless, the Boat Burial People are a fascinating and enigmatic group, and their study has greatly expanded our knowledge of the Bronze Age in Britain and beyond.

interpreting the notion of identity . It is a major doctrine in the Indian philosophy of Nyāya . Syādvāda is used in Indian logic to describe the validity of inference . It is an important doctrine of the Nyaya school of Indian philosophy and is also a major tenet of the Advaita Vedanta school of Hinduism . The doctrine is also used in Buddhist philosophy , especially Yogācāra .
Etymology and meaning
The term syādvāda is composed of two Sanskrit words: syād ( Sanskrit : स्यात् ), which means 'it is so' (in a conditional sense), and vāda ( Sanskrit : वाद ) , which means 'disputation'. The term syādvāda thus means, 'it is so because' or 'it is so if' .
The doctrine of syādvāda is constructed by the Nyāya school as a solution to the problem of identity and difference . The school argues that there is no permanent, immutable identity or difference between any two things. In 1858, the physician Claude Bernard showed that the digestive system could not manufacture protein, so it must be obtained from food. Although the German chemist Justus von Liebig was the first to argue that the chemical bonds in proteins are relatively weak, he failed to establish that proteins must be broken down into their component amino acids. For this, the German biochemist Franz Hoffmann was primarily responsible. Hoffmann showed that the digestibility of certain foods was related to the chemical composition of the proteins in them. For example, proteins extracted from legumes, such as peas, are less digestible than those from meat. Interestingly, Hoffmann was the first to suggest that the protein in food is broken down into its amino acids. In 1876, the German biochemist Wilhelm Kühne suggested that the primary function of protein is to be converted into muscle tissue. Kühne suggested that the body's ability to use protein for this purpose is limited; therefore, a person's diet should be rich in protein. A year later, the American chemist Hermann Wilhelm Vogel concluded that the body is unable to make protein from scratch, but can synthesize amino acids from available protein.
The first textbook on nutrition, written by the Russian Mikhail Ostrogorsky, was published in 1896. Ostrogorsky believed that the body can use proteins as a source of energy, and that the digestion of proteins is performed by the liver. However, he warned that the liver can only process a limited amount of protein. Furthermore, Ostrogorsky believed that the body can make amino acids by combining those from protein with those already present in the body. However, the German biochemist Johann Schardinger later demonstrated that this synthesis could only occur in rare cases and was not a general metabolic process. In 1907, the Russian biochemist Konstantin Albrecht suggested that the body can use carbohydrates as a source of energy, but it can only do this by breaking down the glucose contained in them. Albrecht also suggested that the body can use fat as a source of energy.
In 1908, the German biochemist Max Rubner published his most important work, The Human Unit. In this work, Rubner proposed that the human body can synthesize protein from the amino acids present in it. Rubner also said that the body can use carbohydrates as a source of energy, but can only do this if the glucose contained in them is not used for the synthesis of glycogen. Rubner also suggested that the body can use fat as a source of energy, but only if the fat cells have been broken down to the simplest form of fat: glycerol. On April 12 , 2011 , Legacy Recordings released Bob Dylan in Concert – Brandeis University 1963 , taped at Brandeis University

50 years earlier in 1963.
On April 12, 2011, Legacy Recordings released Bob Dylan in Concert — Brandeis University 1963 , taped at Brandeis University 50 years earlier in 1963. The 24 page booklet accompanying the CD includes liner notes by former Brandeis University student and current Brandeis University Professor Michael Gray, who served on the Brandeis University Board of Trustees from 1979–1993. In the liner notes, he writes,
“ Dylan’s performance is fascinating for many reasons: the music is raw and free of studio asides, he doesn’t seem to have any inhibitions about playing the songs as he first learned them, and he’s very nervous. All of his songs are there, with variations, but no over-played intros and long solos. He uses two guitars and harmonica, a fairly standard configuration, and he’s accompanied on the piano by someone who, as the liner notes to the CD state, ‘doesn’t have his own name.’ That’s me. I was 19 at the time and coming to Brandeis from the UK, so I’m at the concert with a fresh perspective. I can remember clearly that the audience was spellbound, and that the feeling of being in the presence of a genius was overwhelming.”
Gray added, “I’ve spent many years studying the Dylan phenomenon, and it’s clear that the Brandeis concert is one of the key events. The style of the music and the words, and the way they were delivered and interpreted, took folk music into a new area.”
The Brandeis show was Dylan’s first concert appearance in 1963. He had recorded his first album, Bob Dylan, in New York City the previous November. The Brandeis concert, and New York City’s Carnegie Hall concert on April 11, were the first of only a few live performances in 1963, and Dylan would not appear in concert again until 1965’s Newport Folk Festival.
The Brandeis show marked the first time that Dylan had performed “Blowin’ in the Wind,” one of his most famous songs, before a live audience. “Blowin’ in the Wind” was issued on Dylan’s second album, The Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan (1963), which was released on May 27, 1963.

As a studio performer she toured Europe and the United States, where she performed with the likes of Miles Davis, Sonny Rollins, Buddy Rich, Sonny Stitt, and in 1960, with Bill Evans and Hank Jones. She was a member of the Bill Evans Trio from 1961 until 1967, touring widely and recording albums for Riverside Records. Her second album as leader, The Other Side of Simone, helped establish her as a jazz vocalist, and in 1965 she released the critically acclaimed Nessa. In 1968, she performed and recorded in Paris with the French pianist Michel Legrand. Simone appeared in the film Lady Sings the Blues as Billie Holiday; the film itself was a box-office failure, and of the many recordings that resulted from the movie, only one was released by Columbia. She left Verve Records in 1970 and moved to Impulse! Records, where she recorded two albums in 1971 and 1972.
 In 1973, she married David Clark, a former fireman and a close friend of hers who was also recording with her. The couple moved to Los Angeles, where Simone gave birth to their son, Renaldo, in October 1974. In the mid-1970s, she appeared in the television series Kojak and appeared in a role in the film The Sugarland Express. In 1979, she recorded her first gospel album, Let It All Out, for Columbia Records, and she made her last movie appearance, in the film The Jerk, in 1979. In 1985, Simone returned to jazz recording with a live session, Live at the Village Gate, and in 1990 she released the album A New Beginning, which featured her son on guitar.
 In 1988, Simone was diagnosed with breast cancer, and she underwent a mastectomy and chemotherapy. She continued performing and recording, and in 1991 she released a live album, At the Montreux Jazz Festival, and the following year she released the album I Wish You Love, which received an award from the National Association of Jazz Educators. In 1994, she released the album Highway Run and the live album Live at the Village Vanguard, and in 1995 she released the album Live at the House of Blues. Her final studio recording, the gospel album This Is Simone, appeared in 1997, and the following year she appeared on the PBS television special The Concert for World Peace. She died at her home in Los Angeles on 21 August 2003, aged 74.
 Simone's voice is uniquely expressive and infinitely adaptable, whether she is singing about love, about pain, about injustice, or about the virtues of blackness. Her phrasing is unique, never forced or artificial, and she often uses what she called "the rascal voice" to add an extra dimension to her performances. Her vocal style includes a number of traditional jazz inflections, and her technique is so flexible that she can sing with an unadorned simplicity or with intricate musical accompaniment.
 Simone was a unique personality whose life was marked by tragedy and tragedy, but whose spirit was always strong, and whose strong voice was always a source of inspiration. Her music will always remain an important part of the jazz tradition.

It was noted that the work was inspired by a photograph of a horse in the artist’s home in the south of France . The photograph had been taken by the artist’s father , a painter , in the early 1950s . The gates were exhibited at the Halcyon Gallery , London , in November 2013 and were subsequently sold by the gallery . The Halcyon Gallery advertised them as “very rare “. According to the evidence of the artist , the photograph of the black horse was taken by the artist’s father in the early 1950s , and the picture was reproduced on a large canvas by the artist , the work of which was exhibited at the Halcyon Gallery . In its judgment , the High Court unanimously held that the black horse gate was an artistic work within the meaning of section 4( 1 ) of the Copyright , Designs and Patents Act 1988 ( the Act ), and that the reproduction of the photograph by the artist in the early 1950s was an infringement of the artist’s copyright . The Court also held that the reproduction of the picture by the artist was an infringement of the copyright in the photograph . The artist was awarded the full damages for the infringement of the photograph’s copyright , and damages for the infringement of the picture’s copyright , as well as interest and costs .

The definition of leg before wicket ( lbw ) is currently Law 36 in the Laws of Cricket , written by the Marylebone Cricket Club

( MCC ). That Law reads:
a ball shall be adjudged to be "cleanly" "leg before wicket" if it is touched by the batsman so that it would have hit the wicket and gone on to the field of play, and no part of his body line or clothing, except his hand, touches the ground before the ball would have done so.
The ball is adjudged to have hit the wicket if it would have done so when it was passing the batsman's wicket-line, but not if the batsman would have avoided it by any movement of his person or part of his person.
In other words, if the ball hits the wicket while the batsman's leg is behind it, it is out, but if it hits the wicket while the batsman's leg is in front of the ball, it is not out, even if the ball would have hit the stumps but for the batsman's leg. In the first case the ball is said to be "cleanly leg before wicket" ( lbw ), in the second case it is "not out". This terminology is the same as that used in the Law of Fair Play (which does not affect the Law of the Game), but the latter applies only if the ball would have hit the stumps but for the batsman's body or clothing.

To control invasive species, we must understand the factors that cause them to become established and the factors that make them successful. The Black Cuillin, which are mainly composed of basalt and gabbro, include twelve Munros and provide some of the most dramatic and challenging mountain walking in Scotland. The Cuillin Ridge is regarded as one of the greatest walking challenges in the world and the route up Sgurr nan Gillean, a mountain which rises 1018m above the sea, is particularly steep and daunting. The Cuillin Ridge is a spectacular and difficult ridge walk and the normal route is to start from Glen Brittle on the west coast of the Island and walk in a clockwise direction. It is possible to walk the ridge anticlockwise but this involves a long descent to Glen Sligachan. The ascent of Sgurr nan Gillean is the most challenging part of the walk and requires good mountain experience and very good feet. One of the most popular routes, the Sligachan Ridge, is an ascending traverse of the ridge from north to south. It is possible to walk Sgurr nan Gillean (1020m) without ascending the ridge but this involves a long descent to Glen Brittle. The Cuillin is a spectacular mountain area and the highest point is Sgòr na h'Èireann (1080m). The Cuillin are not a suitably equipped mountain area and I would strongly recommend that you reach the summit area by 10am in the summer and 15:00 in the winter. The walk takes about 9 hours and you should allow a day for the walk from Glen Brittle to Glen Sligachan. If you intend walking the Sligachan Ridge, you should allow a further day for the return walk from Glen Sligachan to Glen Brittle. The walk is described as a clockwise walk, starting at Glen Brittle and finishing at Glen Sligachan. The walk from Glen Brittle to Glen Sligachan is described in the additional walk description. The walk from Glen Sligachan to Glen Brittle on the return is also described.

Champlain is a village in Franklin County , Vermont , United States . The population was 1,856 at the 2010 census . The village is in the town of Champlain , but is administratively unincorporated .
Champlain is the eastern terminus of the Lake Champlain Bridge , which crosses the lake from Whitehall, New York , to the north. The bridge is a major artery for east–west traffic in northern New York and Vermont. The village also contains the Champlain Valley Transportation Center , which is served by the Adirondack Northway, a major interstate highway.
The village was named for the French explorer Samuel de Champlain , who landed at the head of the harbor in 1604. Champlain was an early interpreter for the French missionaries who worked among the local Algonquian -speaking population.
As the community grew, the village obtained a post office in 1851, which was named Champlain. The name was officially changed to Champlain Village in 1955, and then to Champlain in 1967.
As of the census of 2000, there were 1,984 people, 796 households, and 574 families residing in the village. The population density was 1,022.8 people per square mile (395.6/km ^{2} ). There were 821 housing units at an average density of 422.0 per square mile (163.1/km ^{2} ). The racial makeup of the village was 98.05% White , 0.05% African American , 0.55% Native American , 0.10% Asian , 0.10% from other races , and 1.14% from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 0.35% of the population.
The median income for a household in the village was $45,000, and the median income for a family was $52,500. Males had a median income of $33,815 versus $25,000 for females. The per capita income for the village was $21,926. About 2.8% of families and 3.7% of the population were below the poverty line , including 2.4% of those under age 18 and 3.8% of those age 65 or over.
According to the United States Census Bureau , the village has a total area of 1.9 square miles (4.9 km ^{2} ), of which, 1.1 square miles (2.8 km ^{2} ) of it is land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km ^{2} ) of it (44.08%) is water.
According to the Köppen Climate Classification system, Champlain has a warm-summer humid continental climate , abbreviated "Dfb" on climate maps.

Wilhelm Busch was born on 15 April 1832 , the first of seven children to the marriage of Henriette Kleine and Friedrich Wilhelm

Busch.
Busch was raised in the village of Werlte in Emsland, North Germany, where his father was a teacher. He lived with his family in nearby Münster from 1846 to 1850, when he went to work for his uncle at a hosiery weaving factory in Paderborn. He left the factory in 1854, after which he worked as a teacher.
Busch was married on 9 September 1854 to Johanna Hartmann. The couple had four children, one of whom died in infancy.
His first published poem was in 1855, and over the next few years he published a number of stories and short poems in various periodicals, including the Rheinische Zeitung and the Münsterische Zeitung. His first book of poems, Die Jugend, was published in 1857. In 1861, his first book of short stories, Der arme Jörg, appeared, followed by two more books of stories: Der krumme Mann (The Crooked Man) in 1864 and Der schlaue Hans (The Clever Hans) in 1875.
In 1863, Busch moved to Berlin to look for work as a writer. He soon met the composer Robert Schumann, who became a friend and mentor. The two men shared a love of music and culture, and Busch often accompanied Schumann on his journeys to the opera and concerts.
In 1864, Busch’s second book of stories, Der krumme Mann, was published. It was followed in 1867 by his first book of satirical drawings, Die lustigen Streiche (The Jolly Pranks). This was followed by a number of other books of drawings, including Die lustigen Streiche (The Jolly Pranks) II, Die lustigen Streiche (The Jolly Pranks) III, and Die lustigen Streiche (The Jolly Pranks) IV.
In 1873, Busch’s most famous book of stories, Das Böse (The Bad), was published. It was followed in 1875 by his second and final book of satirical drawings, Die lustigen Streiche (The Jolly Pranks) V.
Busch was a prolific writer, and his work was widely known and popular in his lifetime. He was also a talented artist, and his drawings were often as popular as his stories.
Busch died on 9 March 1908, in Berlin. He was buried in the cemetery of the Protestant Church in Münster.

In 1114 , the chieftain Wanyan Aguda ( 1068 – 1123 ) united the disparate Jurchen tribes and led a revolt against the Liao . In

1123 he proclaimed himself the Jurchen emperor and established the Jin (Chin) dynasty . He attempted to unite the entire Chinese population under his rule and soon conquered North China . In 1124 he captured the Liao capital and in 1125 captured the Song capital and captured the Chinese emperor of the Song dynasty , Zhao Heng ( 1082 – 1150 ) , and his son Zhao Xu ( 1113 – 1161 ) . [ 17 ] The Song dynasty was virtually destroyed by the Jin dynasty , and the Chinese population of North China , the majority of the population , was enslaved and subjugated . [ 18 ] It is estimated that 10 million Chinese were killed . [ 19 ] The Jin dynasty ended in 1234 , when the Mongolian forces of Genghis Khan conquered China . [ 16 ]
While the Chinese population of North China was enslaved and subjugated , the Mongols treated the Chinese population of Manchuria with relative leniency and thus enabled the viability of the Jurchen population . [ 18 ] The Mongols also tolerated the Manchurian language and customs and were attracted to the Manchurian military tradition . [ 20 ] As a result , in 1207 , the Jurchen , led by Abaoji ( 1161 – 1218 ) , the son of Wanyan Aguda , were invited to join the Mongol empire as a special Mongol military force , the Niohuru . [ 18 ] Abaoji was given the position of the Mongol king 's deputy and was granted the title of Prince . [ 21 ] Abaoji died in 1218 ; his son Wang Hong ( 1169 – 1223 ) was appointed Prince of Jurchen and the first ruler of the Jurchen state . [ 22 ] In 1234 , the Jurchen state was conquered by the Mongols and the dynasty was absorbed into the Mongol empire . [ 23 ]
The Manchurian language was the most important element of the Manchu identity . [ 24 ] In 1617 , the Manchu had become the most powerful tribe in Manchuria . [ 25 ] Over the next two centuries , the Manchus and the Jurchen gradually assimilated and intermarried with the other tribes . [ 25 ] As a result , in the 18th century , the Manchu language and culture declined and the term " Manchu " came to refer to a group of tribes in Manchuria , which included the Jurchen , the Ewenki , the Solon , the Bao'an , the Han , the Naxi , and the Korean minority . [ 24 ] By the 18th century , the Manchu language and culture had disappeared and the Manchu population was assimilated into the Chinese culture . [ 24 ]

The Lyceum continued throughout the 20th century as a centre for the arts in Oldham , and in 1986 the local authority was invit

ed to become a partner in the Lyceum Theatre Company, which had been formed by the Huddersfield Playhouse to establish a professional theatre company in Oldham. Oldham's contribution was focused on training and patronage. The company's first production, at the Lyceum, was a new version of the classic Greek drama The Trojan Women by Euripides, directed by Roger Langridge, and featuring 50 Oldham players.
The Lyceum Theatre Company has continued to perform at the Lyceum with a professional company and in partnership with the local arts council. The company has been particularly associated with productions for young audiences, and with the work of the local youth theatre, which has been the Lyceum's partner for more than 20 years. The theatre has also hosted several national and international theatre companies, including the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre of Scotland.  Since 1988 the Lyceum has been managed by a charitable trust, which has been able to attract major funding from the Arts Council of England and the National Lottery Development Board. In 1992 the Lyceum was given Grade II listed status for its architectural and artistic merit.  The theatre has twice been the subject of redevelopment, first in 1995 when a new state-of-the-art 300-seat studio theatre was built, and again in 2003 when a new £1.5 million theatre, seating 450 people, was built. The latter development has provided the Lyceum with a flexible 400-seat auditorium, a 200-seat studio theatre, bars and a new foyer. The Lyceum Theatre Company continues to work with the local arts council and the youth theatre.
In January 2006 the Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Ian Blair created considerable controversy when he described the media

as `the enemy within'. He later backtracked and apologised. But his remarks were an accurate description of the media's relationship with the police. The relationship has never been easy, and the historic distrust and mistrust which still exists between them is a principal reason why the police often put the public on the defensive, and why they have long been reluctant to cooperate with the media, especially if a story is likely to be controversial or embarrassing. Recent events have shown that the police's reluctance to cooperate with the media can lead to serious consequences. This was the case when the Metropolitan Police Commander in charge of the Hillsborough inquest refused to meet the press, and on the day that the first inquest hearing took place he issued a press release in which he stated that the chairman of the Hillsborough independent panel, Lord Justice Taylor, had stated that the police were not at fault, and that `there is no reason to believe that the police did anything wrong on the day that the football disaster occurred'. The police's refusal to meet the media on the day of the first inquest hearing was an attempt to suppress a story. They could have decided to release the statement at another time and in another way, but their decision to do it on the day of the hearing was intended to intimidate the press into not reporting the facts of the case. They were wrong. The press did report the facts of the case, and the statement was a major embarrassment to the police. More seriously, the chairman of the inquest later demonstrated that the police's press release was a lie. He did not say that the police were not at fault, and he certainly did not state that `there is no reason to believe that the police did anything wrong'. The police's refusal to cooperate with the media, and its decision to suppress the truth, led to the public losing confidence in the police, and to many believing that they were trying to cover up what happened at Hillsborough. For this reason the police have to cooperate with the media, and they have to tell the truth. It is only when they do this that the public will be able to trust them. The police have to show that they are on the side of the public. They have to accept that they have to share information with the media, and that they have to be transparent about the way they handle information. In 1896 Somerset Walpole discovered his son 's horror of the Marlow school and he moved him to the King 's School , Canterbury

1898. At Canterbury he studied classics , mathematics and natural science and in 1900 he was awarded a scholarship to Jesus College , Cambridge. After a year 's training at the Bedford Modern School , Walpole was appointed headmaster in 1902 and remained in post for ten years. For twenty years after this he was a school inspector.
 In 1902 he was introduced to Bertrand Russell by A.N.Whitehead and became his assistant in 1903. Walpole left the Bedford Modern School in 1911. In 1912 he became a Fellow of Trinity College and held the position of Lecturer in Mathematics until 1920. Between 1920 and 1924 he taught mathematics at Bedford High School for Boys.
In 1924 he became Professor of Mathematics and Director of Education at the University of Birmingham and held this position until 1945. He also taught mathematics at the Birmingham College of Education from 1926 to 1931. In 1931 he became the first professor of education at the University of Manchester and held the post until 1945. During his time at Manchester he served as Dean of Education from 1939 to 1945.
During the Second World War he was a member of the Interim Committee on Higher Education, and the post-graduate committee of the University Grants Committee.
After retirement he continued his work as a school inspector and also served as a member of the University Grants Committee until 1960.

The total complement of proteins present at a time in a cell or cell type is known as its proteome , and the study of such larg

The study of proteomics is extensively used in biological research in studying how genes are translated into proteins, and how proteins function in living cells. The study of proteomics is also useful in understanding the function of a disease-causing protein, and for protein engineering and protein expression. Proteomics is based on how proteins are expressed by mRNA, which is encoded by a gene, and how they are modified by their interactions with other proteins and with their environment. The proteome of a cell is divided into substructures, which can be composed of proteins of different functions, or proteins with different properties. The proteome can be divided into substructures, such as extracellular proteome, cytosolic proteome, and organelle proteome. The extracellular proteome is composed of proteins that are secreted from cells. This is the most important part of the proteome, as these proteins are responsible for many functions, such as cell communication, blood clotting, immunity, and cell motility. The cytosolic proteome is composed of proteins that are located inside cells, and plays an important role in regulating the cell's activities. These proteins include enzymes, transporters, and signaling molecules. The organelle proteome plays an important role in the cell's energy production and metabolism. This proteome is composed of proteins that are located within the cell's organelles, such as the mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum. The study of proteomics is complex, as it involves the study of protein structure, protein function, protein interactions, protein expression, and protein modification. Proteomics is a rapidly growing field of research, and it is expected to play an increasingly important role in understanding the function of cells and organisms.

In these ores , the mineral structure of the zinc sulfide contains enough cadmium to produce a concentration of cadmium in the zinc that is high enough to justify its recovery . However , in most cases , the zinc concentrate contains far less cadmium than the zinc ore from which it is produced . At these concentrations , the zinc concentrate is not economically viable for separation ; cadmium is not recovered , and the zinc is sold as a zinc matte . The zinc matte is sold to the primary zinc smelter , where the zinc is refined . The zinc matte contains 45 to 60 percent zinc , 35 to 45 percent iron , and 1.5 to 3.0 percent cadmium . The fieldfare is a migratory species with a palearctic distribution . It breeds in northern Norway , northern Sweden , Finland

and the Kola peninsula (Russia), northern parts of Russia , and in Scandinavia, with highly localized populations in northern Germany , Austria , the Netherlands , and the UK. The species winters in northern Africa , the Middle East , India , and Southeast Asia . This bird is a member of the thrush family and is related to the robin. Fieldfares feed on berries and seeds and are omnivorous. During the winter, they eat mostly fruits, but also insects and other small animals (birds’ eggs, baby birds, and other invertebrates). The fieldfare’s preference is for the fruits of the rowan tree, but it also eats apples, plums, and haws.  It has been suggested that the fieldfare may be partially responsible for the large-scale dispersal of rowan in the UK, [2] as fieldfares are known to be strong seed dispersers. Although the fieldfare is a small bird, it is an aggressive bird that will attack humans if perceived as a threat. It is also known to be aggressive towards other birds and is capable of killing smaller birds.

Hurricane Abby was the only tropical cyclone in the Caribbean Sea during the 1960 Atlantic hurricane season . The second tropic

cyclone numbered by the United States Weather Bureau , the storm developed from a tropical wave east of the Lesser Antilles on September 17, 1960. The system was designated Tropical Storm Abby by the Advisory Office of the United States Weather Bureau on September 17 and later turned into a Category 1 hurricane on September 18. The hurricane then turned towards the west-northwest and, on September 19, crossed the island of Hispaniola . It then moved into the Gulf of Mexico and turned westward. By September 20, Abby had become a minimal hurricane, and later dissipated on September 21.

The system became a tropical depression on September 18 at 09:00 UTC , approximately 180 miles (290 km) east-southeast of Barbados . The depression moved west-northwestward and later turned towards the west. On September 19, the depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Abby as it moved into Hispaniola and later moved towards the southwest. On September 20, Abby turned towards the west, and later weakened into a tropical depression on September 21 before dissipated the following day.

The storm also affected the city of Fort Lauderdale and caused extensive damage to homes. In all, the hurricane caused $150 million in damage in the United States.

Briggs was nominated to run for the governorship on the Whig ticket against the incumbent Democrat Marcus Morton in 1843 . Form

ing a coalition with the anti - Jackson Whigs , Briggs defeated Morton by a narrow margin and served as governor until the end of his term in 1847 . Briggs was defeated for reelection in 1847 by the Democrat John Davis , but he subsequently won the governorship again in 1849 . Edit
Briggs is one of the few surviving Whigs elected to statewide office in Massachusetts during the 1840s . He was a member of the Massachusetts House of Representatives from 1835 to 1843 , and served as a member of the Massachusetts Senate from 1844 to 1847 . Briggs was a staunch supporter of the Mexican - American War , and he signed the 1847 Massachusetts Sinking Fund Bill , which was the state 's first attempt to balance its budget . Briggs also founded the Massachusetts Historical Society in 1846 . Edit
Briggs was a strong supporter of the Compromise of 1850 , which he billed as " a peace - making measure . " He denounced the Know Nothing Party for its anti - Catholicism and anti - foreigner politics , and he called on the Massachusetts legislature in 1855 to investigate the Know Nothings . Briggs supported the Kansas - Nebraska Act of 1854 , which repealed the Missouri Compromise of 1820 , which had prohibited slavery in the territories north of 36 ° 30 ' . Briggs also supported the Dred Scott decision of 1857 . He served as president of the Massachusetts Board of Education from 1861 to 1866 , and was the president of the Massachusetts Historical Society from 1865 until his death . Edit

In 1834 Alkan began his friendship with the Spanish musician Santiago Masarnau , which was to result in an extended and often i

ﬀective correspondence. He would remain in contact with Masarnu until his death in 1908, and at least two of his sonatas were dedicated to him. Masarnau, who had a special interest in the piano, became a friend, correspondent, and a source of information on music. In 1835, Alkan met the Hungarian composer Franz Liszt , who was to become a friend, a source of inspiration and a lifelong companion. Liszt’s friendship with Alkan, which lasted until 1877, was of great importance in the development of Alkan’s style; in particular the Liszt-inﬂuenced Etude in G sharp minor, Op. 35 No. 3 ‘Pour les-Auxerrois’. During the years 1833–1841, Alkan published eleven compositions, including his ﬁrst cello sonata and an etude, dedicated to Liszt. The latter was published in 1841 by Heinrich Vierling (a distinguished music publisher) as a ‘virtual opus’ (opus 0), and was widely praised. The critic A. W. Habeneck applauded the piece, writing: ‘We can say with certainty that this etude will be a brilliant addition to the piano literature and that it will be admired by all musicians’. So great was his respect for Alkan’s work that Habeneck made plans to publish Alkan’s op. 0 with a dedication to Liszt. The etude was also published in the US, where it was praised by the New York Musical Journal . Liszt’s enthusiasm for the work was quite remarkable, as he would come to hate all of Alkan’s work, although Alkan would always remain his friend. In 1841, he dedicated a new etude, op. 1, ‘La Campanella’, to Liszt, who introduced it to his friends and concert-goers and performed it himself. The piece was then published by Vierling, who listed it as op. 1. The piece takes its name from the ‘Campanella’ melody in Liszt’s Piano Sonata in B minor, S. 178, and the two pieces are related, but the melodies are distinct. Alkan’s etude is in the ﬁnal movement of the sonata, and, in Liszt’s words, ‘it is a kind of cantilena’. The New York Musical Journal commented that, in this etude, ‘the composer has gone far beyond the limits of mere virtuosity’. Alkan was to dedicate many compositions to Liszt, including the Sonata in F sharp minor, op. 35, and the Sonata in E flat major, op. 47.

[1] The Union Movement was an ultra - right wing political party that promoted white supremacy , anti - semitism , and anti - immigration policies .[2] Mosley joined the Union Movement after being de - registered in 1967 as a member of the British National Party (BNP) , which later changed its name to the National Front .[3] In 1968 Mosley formally left the Union Movement and joined the BNP .[4]

In 1972 Mosley joined the National Party , a splinter group that advocated a more moderate agenda than the National Front and was less focused on immigration .[5]

In 1973 Mosley left the National Party and rejoined the BNP .[6] He was expelled from the BNP in 1978 , but continued to support it .[7] In 1980 Mosley resigned from the BNP and formed his own political party , the British League of Rights , which was formed by a merger of the League of Rights and League of Imperial Union .[8] He re - joined the BNP in 1983 , but left again in 1987 to form the New British Union (NBU) , which was better known as the British National Party .[9] Mosley was elected the leader of this party in 1988 .[10]

He was elected to the European Parliament in 1999 , and was re - elected in 2004 , 2009 and 2014 .[11] He was the only British MEP to be elected in every single European election from 1979 to 2019 .[12] He ran as a candidate for the London mayoral election in 2000 and 2008 , but was unsuccessful .[13]

In 2014 Mosley announced that he would retire from the European Parliament , but would continue to lead the BNP .[14] He did not stand for election to the European Parliament in 2019 .[15]

In 2017 , Mosley announced that he had decided to retire from active politics and from his party , the BNP , and would devote himself to writing and to his private life .[16]
During the battle , the British Commonwealth logistic system proved robust enough to bear the strain of the fighting without se

The British Commonwealth Logistic System , in principle , had the capacity to provide the supplies and services that were required .
The Allied supply problem was the result mainly of bad planning and the failure to anticipate the magnitude of the logistic effort .

It is often diagnosed in people over the age of 60 , and is less common in children and younger adults . To diagnose acute myeloid leukemia , a blood test and bone marrow biopsy is usually performed . The image of the Lord of Cabeza (Señor de Cabeza) was brought there from the Church of San Miguel in Montemayor in 1568, at the request of the parish priest, Juan de Yepes. The chapel was enlarged in 1664 and 1769. Painting and sculpture Since 1914, the Chapel of Saint Joseph has been a national monument. It was declared a Site of Cultural Interest in 1931. The Chapel of Saint Joseph contains the image of Our Lord of Cabeza (Señor de Cabeza), the patron saint of the city of Montemayor. The image is kept in a side chapel, and the remains of Joaquín Antonio de Pereda y Salgado (1848–1922), a 19th century painter, are also kept there. . The Chapel is decorated with paintings by Alonso Cano (1610–1667), a 17th century Colombian painter, and Pedro de Campaña (1586–1657), a Spanish painter. The film was born of a simple idea: what would happen if a car accident happened in a mall on Thanksgiving Day, and how the lives of the people affected by that accident would be affected by it? Over four years, Anderson wrote over 300 pages of script, focusing on a core group of characters and then expanding their stories to encompass a wider world. In the end, Magnolia was a 25-character story, with 6,000 pages of dialogue and 100,000 words. The film featured, in addition to the core group, a number of cameo appearances by members of Anderson’s family, among them his mother, brother, and sister. The film also featured a score by Jon Brion , who would go on to produce Anderson’s next film.
Magnolia premiered on October 13, 1999, at the New York Film Festival with a 20-minute screening followed by a 60-minute Q & A with Anderson. Although it was not among the festival’s most popular entries, both critics and audiences seemed to embrace the film. The film was generally well received by critics and was nominated for five Academy Awards (for Best Picture, Director, Screenplay, Original Score, and Cinematography), although it lost the last four to American Beauty . Anderson was nominated for a Golden Globe Award and won the 2000 Independent Spirit Award for Best Director.
Magnolia was released in theaters on December 22, 1999, where it grossed $7.3 million, almost double the amount of Boogie Nights ’s opening weekend in 1997. In 2017, the film was included in the Library of Congress’s National Film Registry, which recognizes films that have been deemed “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.”

When a judge is influenced by an extrinsic factor, an "extrinsic influence" is said to have tainted the judge's impartiality. An extrinsic influence is one that is not attributable to a judge's character, mental condition, or personal interests. An extrinsic influence may be either a personal one, such as an affection or hostility between the judge and an individual, or an external one, such as a substantial financial interest in any party to the case or a threat of imprisonment for an unrelated crime. The presence or absence of an extrinsic influence is a question of fact. We must determine whether the forensic evidence was sufficient for a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that the judge's impartiality was "actually and perhaps prejudicially affected" by an extrinsic influence. United States v. Knox , 441 F.3d 340, 347 (4th Cir. 2006) (quoting United States v. Peltier , 166 F.3d 999, 1006 (4th Cir. 1999)). We review for clear error the district court's factual findings concerning extrinsic influences on the judge's impartiality. United States v. Sowles , 293 F.3d 314, 328 (4th Cir. 2002).
On appeal, Defendants argue that the district court erred in concluding that the judge's impartiality was not tainted by extrinsic influences. Specifically, Defendants claim that the district court improperly focused on the judge's extrajudicial comments concerning the 2007 murder of Faulkner and that these comments were not a proper subject for inquiry on remand. The abandoned house is in a state of disrepair and is earmarked by the City Council for demolition . To the indifference of the

neighbors and the City Council, the house remains standing, like one of the many statues of the city, but in this case a real statue of a house, or rather of a piece of house, a fragment of the past, a memory of the city.
The house, which has been damaged by fire, is on a street that is not particularly frequented by passers-by, although it is not far from the city center. It was here, in the middle of the night, that the photographer and I found the house, abandoned, the windows broken, the doors ajar . A few hours later, the sun rose and the walls of the house, which had been hiding in the shadow of its past, began to be illuminated by a light as bright as the day of our arrival. The white light of the sun, the light that was poured into the house, transformed it into something strange: a lost house, a house that had become a statue, a house that had been relegated to the status of a piece of the past. 
 The house of the street has become a monument to the house, a house that was once lived in by people, but was abandoned, and is now a memory of the city. The city, which is always full of past and present, is always full of history, and it is up to the artist to capture those moments and to transform them into something beautiful, to give them a new meaning .

" Fergalicious " is a song by American singer-songwriter Fergie from her debut solo studio album, The Dutchess (2006). It was released as the album's lead single on August 28, 2006, by A&M Records. "Fergalicious" is a midtempo "sleazy, sexy, and soulful" tune that features Fergie's "signature, brassy delivery" and was compared to the work of Sam Cooke. The song received mostly positive reviews. Phil Harrison of Timeout called "Freakum Dress" a magnificent production thanks to its "slinky, seductive" vocals and the songwriting of its co-writers. Sarah Rodman of The Boston Globe called it "a throwback to the kind of R&B that can only be done by a black woman. "Fergalicious" was performed live by Fergie on several occasions and included in live shows of her tours. The song was included in the soundtracks of the films "The Holiday", "Glory Road", "The Last Kiss", and "Bridge to Terabithia". The video version of the single features a 90-second intro clip of "Glamorous", the following is a 15-second clip of "Glamorous" featuring a cameos of Fergie, Akon, Jay-Z and Foxy Brown. "Fergalicious" debuted at number forty-two on the Billboard Hot 100 and reached the top five on the Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart. It also peaked at the number four position on the Hot Dance Club Songs chart. "Fergalicious" has sold 2.4 million units in the United States as of June 2007. The song received a nomination at the 2007 Grammy Awards for Best Rap/Sung Collaboration. "Fergalicious" was nominated for Favorite R&B Female Single at the 2007 American Music Awards.

ormism.
 He was a son of Judah Beer and a grandson of Schalom Beer (d. 1857), a Hungarian Jew who had fled to Berlin in 1828 and the father of a large family of children. Judah Beer himself was married in 1857 to the daughter of Jakob Wohlwill, a prosperous merchant of the city, and had two sons and two daughters. In 1861, on the occasion of his father-in-law's death, Beer acquired his business operations and became a member of the board of the chamber of commerce as a representative of the German Jews. In 1869 he succeeded his father-in-law as owner of the firm Wohlwill & Cie. and was appointed managing director of the company. He was also a member of the board of the Verein zur Förderung des deutschen Handels and a member of the city council of Berlin.
 Judah Beer was also a member of the Jewish community and had been one of the initiators of the attempted revision of the communal constitution of 1855. He was the chairman of the committee for the translation of the Torah and was a member of the board of the community. He was a member of the delegation of the Berlin community to the Allgemeiner Wissenschaftlicher Congress of German Jews in Frankfurt in 1869 and was a representative of the community at the general assembly of the Jewish community in the 1870s. In 1881 he became president of the community and in 1887 a member of the Berlin city council.
 Judah Beer was also known for his philanthropy. He was a member of the board of the Verein zur Förderung der deutschen Wohlfahrtspflege, a member of the committee for aid to the destitute, and in 1871 he was one of the founders of the Jewish congregation of St. John in Berlin. Most proteins , ribosomal subunits , and some DNAs are transported through the pore complexes in a process mediated by a family

of solute transporters called TAPS (tetratricopeptide repeats associated with protein import ). The TAPS family comprises four members (TAP1 , TAP2, TAP3, and TAP4) that are localized to the pore complexes of mitochondria (TAP1 and TAP2) and chloroplasts (TAP3 and TAP4). Mitochondrial and chloroplast TAPS proteins are localized in the inner membrane (TAP1, TAP2, TAP3), the outer membrane (TAP4), and the intermembrane space (TAP1). TAP1 and TAP2 associate with mitochondrial import receptors , which mediate the import of proteins and RNAs from the cytosol. TAP4 appears to be involved in chloroplast movement during chloroplast biogenesis. TAP3 may be involved in the transport of proteins and their targeted assembly into the chloroplast. TAP4 interacts with the small subunit of the chloroplast ribosome, and may be involved in the assembly of proteins into the chloroplast, as well as in chloroplast movement during biogenesis.

+ == Jupiter's Moons ==
+ Jupiter has 63 known moons. Jovian moons are divided into two categories: inner moons and outer moons. Inner moons are closer to Jupiter than 5 times the distance of Jupiter from the Sun. The inner moons are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto; they are also known as the Galilean moons. The outer moons are all farther than 5 times the distance of Jupiter from the Sun. The outer moons are known as the Himalia group, Amalthea group, Carme group, and Pasiphae group.
+ === Galilean Moons ===
+ The Galilean moons are named after characters from Greek mythology. The order of the moons starts with the closest to Jupiter and ends with the farthest. Io is the moon closest to Jupiter. Io, the innermost moon of the Galilean moons, orbits Jupiter in about 42 hours (1.8 days). The next moon to Io is Europa, which orbits Jupiter in about 3.5 days. Europa is the second closest moon to Jupiter. The third closest moon to Jupiter is Ganymede. Ganymede orbits Jupiter every 7.2 days. The outermost and farthest Galilean moon is Callisto. Callisto orbits Jupiter in 16.7 days.
+ = ==Himalia Group ===
+ The Himalia group is a group of 5 low-inclination synchronous irregular moons, which means that they orbit Jupiter on the same side of Jupiter. The Himalia group was named after Himalia, the mother of the Titan Prometheus, in Greek mythology. Himalia was the first discovered moon of Jupiter, discovered in 1904. The Himalia group includes Himalia, Lysithea, Elara, S/2000 J 11 and S/2003 J 2.
+ = == Amalthea Group ===
+ The Amalthea group consists of 2 small inner moons that orbit Jupiter on the same side of Jupiter. They are named after Amalthea, a goat who nursed the infant Zeus in Greek mythology. The Amalthea group includes Amalthea and Thebe.
+ = == Carme Group ===
+ The Carme group is a small group of 3 low-inclination synchronous irregular moons, which means that they orbit Jupiter on the same side of Jupiter. The Carme group was named after Carme, a nymph in Greek mythology. The Carme group includes Carme, Ersa, and Erigone.
+ = == Pasiphae Group ===
+ The Pasiphae group consists of 3 small moons that orbit Jupiter on the same side of Jupiter. The Pasiphae group was named after Pasiphae, a Queen of Crete in Greek mythology. The Pasiphae group includes Pasiphae, Sinope, and S/2003 J 4.
+ === Other Moons ===
+ Other moons discovered by the Galileo spacecraft include Adrastea, Metis, Amalthea, Thebe, Leda, and Ananke.

[ edit ] Stoke City McCall was appointed manager of Stoke City on 14 January 2004 after Graham Potter had been sacked earlier on the same day . Stoke were seventh in the Championship on 14 January 2004 , but the club had been without a manager for 14 days . McCall signed a one - year deal , with a one - year option to extend . In his first full season in charge , he guided Stoke to the play - off final and promotion to the Premier League . In 2006 , McCall signed a new three - year contract . It was extended by one year in 2009 , and a further year in 2011 . [ edit ] Blackburn Rovers McCall was appointed Blackburn Rovers manager on 14 April 2012 , after previous manager Steve Kean was sacked . The club were in 18th place in the Premier League on the day he was appointed . He signed a two - year contract which would have kept him at Ewood Park until the end of the 2013–14 season . The club were relegated to the Championship in 2012 , but the club's fortunes improved under McCall , who led the club to a mid - table finish in the second tier during the 2012–13 season . In 2013–14 , the club finished second in the Championship and were promoted back to the Premier League . [ edit ] Republic of Ireland McCall was appointed manager of the Republic of Ireland on 17 May 2013 , following the resignation of Giovanni Trapattoni . He signed a three - year contract , and made his first competitive game in charge on 7 September 2013 , a 2–0 defeat to Germany , in the 2014 FIFA World Cup qualifying . McCall was sacked on 21 October 2014 . The Badinter Arbitration Committee was set up by the Council of Ministers of the European Economic Community ( EEC ) on 27 Augu

s t 1988 in order to clarify the law of the EEC and its Member States in the field of family law and more particularly in the case of the dissolution of marriages. The Committee, which is chaired by Professor Badinter, is composed of five permanent members and five alternates. The members of the Committee have been appointed by the Council of Ministers of the EEC and the governments of the Member States.
 The Committee was called upon to examine the following case : the applicant seeks the annulment of the decree of divorce granted by the Luxembourg court on 27 April 1987. The applicant is an Italian national who had been living in Luxembourg for more than ten years and who was granted a divorce on the ground of the incompatibility of her marriage with the principles of the Italian legal system. The applicant was given custody of the two minor children of the marriage. The divorce decree was challenged in the courts of Italy. The application for annulment was dismissed on 7 May 1991 and a final decision was delivered by the Court of Cassation on 23 July 1991, which was to the effect that the Luxembourg court had committed an error of law in deciding that the incompatibility of her marriage with the principles of the Italian legal system was a sufficient ground for divorce in the case of a Luxembourg national.
 In the light of the above, the applicant was granted leave to apply to the Committee for the annulment of the Luxembourg decree of divorce. The Committee, in its decision of 7 Decem ber 1991, held that the Luxembourg court had not made an error of law since the Italian legal system did not require a marriage to be annulled in order for the marriage to be declared null and void in accordance with the provisions of the Luxembourg Family Code. It therefore rejected the applicant’s application.
 In this action, the applicant seeks the annulment of the decision of the Badinter Arbitration Committee on the grounds that the Luxembourg court had made an error of law when it had found that the Italian legal system did not require an annulment of the marriage. The applicant also submits that, in any event, the Italian legal system did require an annulment of the marriage, thus justifying the Luxembourg court in refusing to grant a divorce.
 Before answering the applicant’s arguments, the Court must first consider whether the Luxembourg court had jurisdiction to rule on the applicant’s application for annulment of the divorce decree.
 The Court notes that, in the circumstances of the present case, the Luxembourg court had jurisdiction to rule on the applicant’s application for annulment of the divorce decree. The Luxembourg court had jurisdiction by virtue of the provisions of Article 38(1) of the Luxembourg Family Code, which provide that a decision to grant a divorce may be challenged, at the request of the applicant, in the courts which granted the decree. The Luxembourg court also had jurisdiction by virtue of the provisions of Article 40 of the Luxembourg Family Code, which provide that the Luxembourg court may rule on the question of the annulment of a decree of divorce only if such a question has arisen in the course of a case before that court. The Luxembourg court had jurisdiction in the present case, since the applicant had requested the annulment of the divorce decree in the course of the proceedings before the Luxembourg court.

The Galveston Railway , originally established and named in 1854 as the Galveston Wharf and Cotton Press Company , is a Class I

railroad that provides freight and commuter rail services. The company's headquarters are located in Galveston, Texas .
The Galveston Railway  originated as the Galveston Bay, Harrisburg and Galveston Railroad in 1854, beginning operations in 1859. The line ran from Beach City, Texas (now Galveston), to Harrisburg (now Houston), a trip that took 14 hours. In 1870, the line was purchased by the Texas Central Railroad and the name was changed to the Texas Central and Galveston Railway .
In 1883, the Houston and Texas Central Railway took over the Texas Central and Galveston Railway. Afterward, the Houston and Texas Central Railway was renamed the Houston and Texas Central Railroad in 1884. On October 1, 1893, the Houston and Texas Central Railroad was renamed the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway .
In its first 40 years, the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway was primarily a freight railroad. In 1934, it made its first excursion train, the "Excursion Limited", which was a daily service from Houston to Galveston.
On June 1, 1955, the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway became a subsidiary railroad of the Southern Pacific Railroad . The Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway was renamed the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railroad .
In 1965, the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railroad was purchased by the Missouri Pacific Railroad , which was itself purchased by the Union Pacific Railroad in 1982. The Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railroad was renamed the Galveston Railway . In 2006, the Galveston Railway was purchased by Fortress Investment Group , a private equity firm.
In 2007, the Galveston Railway was acquired by OmniTRAX , a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway , which operates the line under its own name. The Houston Area Rapid Transit provides commuter rail service on the line between Downtown Houston and Galveston Island.
The Galveston Railway is a Class I railroad, the highest classification of railroad in the United States, and the only Class I railroad in Texas. It is the second-largest railroad in Texas in terms of revenue (behind the Union Pacific Railroad ) and the third largest railroad in terms of tonnage (behind the Union Pacific Railroad and the BNSF Railway ).
The Galveston Railway owns and operates 318 miles (510 km) of track in Texas. Of that total, 192 miles (310 km) of track is used for freight operations, and 126 miles (203 km) of track is used for passenger operations. The Galveston Railway has 1,600 diesel locomotives and 12,400 freight cars. It operates 12 locomotive maintenance facilities and 40 freight yards.

ooensis ) were combined into a single species , the Ningaloo maskray , and its synonymy with the plain maskray was noted. A 2014 study  conducted by the Western Australian Museum based on cytology and molecular genetics found that the plain maskray and Ningaloo maskray were distinct species. The Ningaloo maskray was restricted to waters within a 30 km radius of Ningaloo Reef, along with a third species, the Ningaloo Reef maskray ( N. reefensis ).  The plain maskray ( N. pinnata ) has been recorded off Ningaloo Reef and the Ningaloo Reef maskray ( N. reefensis ) may have been intermixed with plain maskray in some areas, but the Ningaloo Reef maskray is a distinct species.  The Ningaloo Reef maskray is the only species of the genus in the Indian Ocean and has been recorded from the Kimberley in Western Australia to the Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal.
