The Great Coastal hurricane of 1806 was first noted far east of the Lesser Antilles on 17 August . Weather historian David M. L

ittauer in his "A History of Atlantic Tropical Cyclones" (John Wiley & Sons, 2006) states that the hurricane was the first known "superstorm" in the North Atlantic basin. It moved eastward but weaken to a tropical depression by 20 August. The storm then became a post-tropical cyclone by 21 August . Hurricane Juan of 2003 was the first named storm to have the name Juan after the Atlantic hurricane season of 2003 was cancelled due to the 2003 North American monsoon season . On August 10, 2012, Hurricane Gillian strengthened to a Category 3 hurricane just east of the Lesser Antilles. As of August 11, the storm was downgraded to a tropical storm. In the 2012 Atlantic hurricane season, a total of 15 storms formed. Nine of these storms reached at least tropical storm strength (65 mph winds or greater). Nine of these storms became hurricanes (at least 74 mph winds or greater). Six of these hurricanes became major hurricanes (category 3, 4, or 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale). One storm, Tropical Storm Debby, became the first storm of the 2012 Atlantic hurricane season on May 27, 2012. It was the earliest date for the formation of a named storm since the 1933 Atlantic hurricane season. At the time, it was the earliest date for the formation of any tropical cyclone in the Atlantic basin since the 1933 Atlantic hurricane season. In September 2012, a tropical wave in the central tropical Atlantic, that developed into Tropical Storm Leslie on September 18, 2012. Leslie became the first named storm of the 2012 Atlantic hurricane season to form after the official start of the season, August 1. Leslie was also the first named storm of the 2012 Atlantic hurricane season to form south of 20 °N , and was also the first storm to form east of 30 °W . Leslie was the 11th storm of the season, and the first to make landfall in the United States. Upon making landfall along the North Carolina coast, Leslie was downgraded to a tropical depression. It then dissipated over the Appalachian Mountains. Tropical Storm Nadine formed on September 15, 2012, and was the 12th named storm of the 2012 season. It was the first named storm to reach hurricane strength, but was downgraded to a tropical storm before making landfall. Tropical Storm Ophelia strengthened to hurricane strength before it made landfall in Bermuda on September 30, 2012. It was the first tropical storm to form east of 30 °W since Tropical Storm Erika formed in 2000. Ophelia was the 14th named storm of the season, and the second to reach hurricane strength. It was also the first hurricane to form east of 30 °W since Hurricane Erin of 1995. Ophelia was the first storm to form in the Atlantic basin to name after an animal, as well as the first tropical cyclone to form in September to name after an animal. Tropical Storm Pablo became the 15th storm of the season, and the first to name after a location (Pablo is the Spanish name of the Canary Islands). Pablo formed on October 7, 2012, and was the first storm to form west of the Lesser Antilles since Tropical Storm Isaac of 2012. Pablo was the first storm to form in the Atlantic basin to name after a location. Pablo was also the last tropical cyclone to form in the Atlantic basin, and the last storm of the season to name after an animal. The 2012 Atlantic hurricane season was the first season since 1969 in which a tropical storm formed south of 20 °N. It was also the first season since 1961, in which a tropical storm formed east of 30 °W.

Mozambique was marked by large disparities between the wealthy Portuguese and the majority of the large rural indigenous Africa

population, which was divided into tribes and ethnic groups. In 1915, the Portuguese government awarded to the Portuguese-born David Livingstone Cunha Maia, the concession for the exploitation of gold mines in the region that would later be called the Zambezia Province. The concession was based on a British discovery made by the Scottish explorer David Livingstone in 1863.
 The mineworkers were classified as "indigenas" and as such were subjected to a large number of discriminatory practices. The Portuguese legislation of the time recognized the "indigenas" as a separate social class, and their legal status was that of "third grade citizens" with no right to vote or hold public office. Despite the concession being granted to a Portuguese citizen in 1915, the exploitation of the mines was not really started until 1951, when the Portuguese government awarded to the British firm BHP a concession for the exploitation of the mines. In 1953, the new company started the exploitation of the mines, which were located in the regions of Tete and Zambezia, in the present day provinces of Tete and Zambezia.
 The exploitation of the mines was definitely started at the beginning of the 1960's. By 1963, the Portuguese government had already started a large public works campaign with the aim of building roads and railways, and constructing a dam to produce electricity.
 The government also started the construction of a port in the northern port city of Nacala. In 1970, a new road was built linking Tete and Mocuba, and a railway that would connect the mines with the sea was completed in 1977, but with the construction of the railway the exploitation of the mines fell into decline. In 1974, the Portuguese government nationalized the gold mines, but the company was still heavily indebted.

Antibodies are protein components of an adaptive immune system whose main function is to bind antigens , or foreign substances

that enter the body. Antigen binding induces a change in the three-dimensional shape of the antibody, which leads to creation of a specific immune response. The antibodies recognize only a certain antigen and bind to it with high affinity. Antibodies belong to a class of proteins called immunoglobulins, and comprise five different classes (IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, IgM) and two subclasses of each (i.e., 10 Ig classes in total).  Antibodies can be produced by both the innate and adaptive immune systems. Innate immune antibodies—called immunoglobulins—are produced by the B cells of the immune system and include IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM. They are found throughout the body as part of the complement system and are also present at mucosal surfaces.  Adaptive immune antibodies, also called immunoglobulins, are produced by the B cells of the immune system and are produced in response to an antigen. This response is specifically tailored to each antigen and is not present in the body prior to exposure to the antigen. The adaptive immune system consists of memory B cells (which can produce antibodies as a part of the humoral immune response), memory T cells (which can produce antibodies as a part of the cellular immune response), and helper T cells (which can activate both B cells and memory T cells). Adaptive immune antibodies include IgG, IgM, and IgA.  The main function of antibodies is to bind antigens. Antibodies are produced by the B cells of the immune system in response to exposure to an antigen. Antibodies are involved in the immune response, which can cause inflammation of the affected area. Antibodies can cause the immune system to recognize the antigen, and can cause the antigen to be removed from the body.

A principal destination along the former Oldham Loop Line , Oldham once had six railway stations but this was reduced to three

In 1964 the station was redeveloped, with a new platform at the former down end of the station and the old down platform was extended to the new up platform at the former up end of the station. The station was designed by the MS&LR engineer Thomas Wilson, who used the same design for the stations at Ashton-under-Lyne and Dukinfield.

The station has been proposed as a stopping point on the Greater Manchester Metro, however there are no plans to build a new station.

Charles Eaton , OBE , AFC ( 21 December 1895 – 12 November 1979 ) was a senior officer and aviator in the Royal Australian Air

Force (RAAF) during World War II . He was the only Australian to earn the DFC & Bar and AFC & Bar on the same aircraft.
Eaton enlisted in the AIF in 1915 and was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the 3rd Battalion on 17 November 1915 . He served on Gallipoli from April 1915 until April 1916 , when he was transferred to the RAAF in July 1916 . He served in the United Kingdom from 1916 to 1919 , and in Egypt from 1919 to 1920 .
Eaton was commissioned as a flight lieutenant in the RAAF on 1 March 1921 , and served in the United Kingdom from 1921 to 1923 , and on the Gold Coast from 1923 to 1925 . He was promoted to flight commander on 1 March 1924 , and to squadron leader on 1 July 1925 . He was promoted to wing commander on 1 July 1932 , and to group captain on 1 March 1935 . He was promoted to air commodore on 1 July 1939 , and to air vice-marshal on 1 April 1940 . He was promoted to air marshal on 1 July 1941 , and retired on 1 October 1943 .
Eaton was appointed as a member of the Order of the British Empire in the 1935 Queen's Birthday Honours , and was awarded the Air Force Cross in the 1940 New Year Honours . He was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for gallantry on 5 June 1942 . This was gazetted as a bar to his DFC on 28 July 1944 . He was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross (Bar) on 6 December 1945 . This was gazetted as a bar to his DFC & Bar on 5 April 1946 . He was appointed as a Member of the Order of the British Empire in the 1945 King's Birthday Honours , and was awarded the Air Force Cross (Bar) on 28 September 1946 . This was gazetted as a bar to his AFC & Bar on 12 October 1946 .
Eaton was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire in the 1946 New Year Honours , and was promoted to acting air chief marshal on 1 January 1946 . He was promoted to air chief marshal on 1 January 1947 . He was invested as an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in the 1947 Queen's Birthday Honours .
Eaton married Jean Mary Flanagan in 1930 , and had a daughter, Mary Elizabeth, and a son, John Charles. He died in 1979 .
The National Library of Australia holds a collection of Eaton's papers , including his memoirs.
Eaton was the subject of a 1979 Australian Broadcasting Commission radio documentary , Charles Eaton , by his daughter Mary.

New York State Route 38 ( NY 38 ) is a north – south state highway in the Finger Lakes region of New York in the United States

38 is one of the shortest numbered routes in New York, running for a distance of 6.29 long. The route travels from Interstate 90 ( I-90 ) in the town of Waterloo north to State Route 14 ( SR 14 ) in the town of Hector, where it joins with U.S. Route 20 ( US 20 ). NY 38 was legislatively assigned in 1930 and was originally a part of the former US 20. From its south end to the town of Newark, NY 38 was part of the former US 20. From the town of Newark to the town of Hector, NY 38 was part of the former NY 14B. From Hector to the north end, NY 38 was part of the former NY 14. NY 38 was extended in 1957 and 1965. In 1993, NY 38 was briefly extended south to NY 5 , which was realigned onto NY 38, but the realignment was removed in 2001. NY 38 was designated as a U.S. Highway in 1926 and would become part of NY 38 in 1930. NY 38 was renumbered from NY 38A in 1930, but the route was changed to what it is now. NY 38 was extended north in 1957 and 1965. In 1993, NY 38 was extended south to NY 5 and realigned onto NY 38, but the realignment was removed in 2001. In 1996, NY 38 was extended south to SR 5. Today, NY 38 is the main transportation link between the Finger Lakes and the greater Rochester area. Route description The southern terminus of NY 38 is at an interchange with I-90 in the town of Waterloo. The route heads northward as a four-lane divided highway, passing through the community of Waterloo. The route intersects and overlaps with NY 414. NY 38 continues northward, passing through the town of Newark. NY 38 intersects and overlaps with NY 414, NY 272, and NY 414 again. The route continues northward, leaving the city of Rochester behind and traveling northward through New York State's Finger Lakes region. The route passes through the towns of Victor, Manchester, and Hector before meeting its northern terminus at an interchange with SR 14. History NY 38 was legislatively assigned in 1930 as a part of the former US 20. From the town of Newark to the town of Hector, NY 38 was a part of the former NY 14B, and from Hector to the north end, NY 38 was a part of the former NY 14. NY 38 was extended north into Victor in 1957 and Manchester in 1965. In 1993, NY 38 was extended south to NY 5, which was realigned onto NY 38, but the realignment was removed in 2001. NY 38 was designated as a U.S. Highway in 1926 and would become part of NY 38 in 1930. NY 38 was renumbered from NY 38A in 1930, but the route was changed to what it is now. NY 38 was extended north in 1957 and 1965. In 1993, NY 38 was extended south to NY 5 and realigned onto NY 38, but the realignment was removed in 2001. In 1996, NY 38 was extended south to SR 5. Today, NY 38 is the main transportation link between the Finger Lakes and the greater Rochester area. The First World War , also known as the Great War , was a global military conflict originating in Europe , that lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918 . More than 70 million military personnel , including 60 million Europeans , were mobilised in one of the largest wars in history . Over nine million combatants and seven million civilians died as a result of the war , a casualty rate exacerbated by the belligerents ' technological and industrial sophistication , and the tactical stalemate caused by gruelling trench warfare . It was one of the deadliest conflicts in history , and precipitated major political change , including the Revolutions of 1917–1923 in many of the nations involved . Unresolved rivalries at the end of the First World War and failure of the postwar conference to address them contributed to the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 . The First World War began on 28 July 1914 , when Austria - Hungary declared war on Serbia , and was a result of the complex set of diplomatic events that had been unfolding in Eastern Europe since the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria - Hungary in June 1914 . A series of political declarations followed thereafter, all ultimately resulting in the declaration of war by at least one European power against another . The war was formally limited to the Europeans through a series of simultaneous declarations of neutrality by the United States , Japan , and the Ottoman Empire in November 1914 . In the following four years , the combatants destroyed cities , towns , village , cultivated land , infrastructure , and forests , and killed millions of civilians and soldiers . Moreover , technology , politics , and ideas also changed significantly . Comair Flight 5191 , marketed as Delta Connection Flight 5191 , was a scheduled United States ( US ) domestic passenger flight

operated by Comair for Delta Air Lines and which crashed upon take-off on 12 August 2006 at the Blue Grass Airport ( IATA : LEX , ICAO : KLEX ) in Lexington, Kentucky , United States . The Beechcraft 1900D , registration Number N190CM, operated by Comair , crashed as it tried to take off from the wrong runway number , 28L rather than the intended runway number 28R . The runway was 3,500 feet (1,064 m) shorter than the length of the aircraft , resulting in a failed take-off and subsequent crash . Nine people were killed , including the pilot . The National Transportation Safety Board ( NTSB ) determined that the events leading to the crash were a result of pilot error . The cause of the crash was attributed to the pilot's failure to properly read the airport layout and the resulting error in picking the wrong runway for take-off . The pilot was not aware that the runway identification was changed from 28L to 28R around 1999 . The crew had only recently been trained to use the runway number change and had not practiced the new procedure . The crash was the deadliest in Comair 's history . It was leased from Beechcraft International , a subsidiary of Textron Aviation , the aircraft 's manufacturer . The Beechcraft 1900D is a twin-engine turboprop passenger aircraft , seating 19 passengers . It was the first aircraft type used by Comair . Prior to the crash , the aircraft had flown 22,000 hours and had completed 9,500 cycles . The crew consisted of Captain David A. Hayes , 43 years old , with 14,509 flight hours , and First Officer Richard H. Cole , 40 years old , with 5,856 flight hours . The plane was scheduled to depart Lexington at 8: 08 a.m. EST . Its destination was Milwaukee , Wisconsin . According to witness accounts, the aircraft was not moving on the taxiway when the crew apparently attempted to take off from the wrong runway . As a result of the failed take-off , the aircraft crashed and caught fire . The crash occurred 1, 600 feet (490 m) from the end of the runway , in a wooded area , near the airport . The aircraft was consumed by fire . There were nine fatalities , including the pilot and passengers . Five survivors were taken to hospital . The National Transportation Safety Board ( NTSB ) was called to investigate the crash . The NTSB determined that the probable cause of the crash was the crew 's failure to read the airport layout , resulting in the crew 's failure to pick the correct runway for take-off . To perform in vitro analysis , a protein must be purified away from other cellular components . This process usually begins with the protein's isolation from cells in a lysis buffer and then its separation from other cellular components by methods such as chromatography . Proteins are separated by size and shape using gel electrophoresis , for example . The proteins are separated by their net positive or negative charge and then detected by staining the gel with a dye such as Coomassie . The proteins can also be detected by western blotting , a technique that involves the separation of proteins that are electrophoretically transferred to a membrane .

The multiplayer component of Journey was designed to facilitate cooperation between players without forcing it , and without al

lying or attacking them. The game invites players to work together for mutual benefit, and to take care of one another as the experience progresses. The players' goals are the same, and their paths are parallel, so they are not forced together or forced apart. The game offers no options for local multiplayer, but players can invite friends to join them or play with strangers. Many of the events in the game are designed to reduce the sense of alienation: players have no idea who is with them or where they came from. The landscape is a shared space, and players must navigate it together. The player character has no weapons, no armor, no communication device, and no visible means of identifying the other player(s). This anonymity prevents the formation of alliances and reduces the possibility of conflict. When players meet, they share a common goal: to reach the top of the mountain. The mountain is visible from the player's starting point, but it is not possible to reach it immediately. As players climb, they gradually become aware of the mountain and of other players. The game does not tell them when they reach the summit, and it does not expose them to the dangers of other players. When players reach a common location, they are often still blind to their fellow players. The game makes no attempt to explain how players will be helped, how they will be found, or when they will reach their destination. Much of the gameplay requires players to work together, but the game does not force them to do so , and it does not prevent them from working alone. The game also does not tell them the time of day or night; players must rely on their own senses to determine whether it is daylight or nighttime. The North / South Ministerial Council is an institution through which ministers from the Government of Ireland and the Northern

Ireland Executive cooperate on a number of cross-border issues. It was established under the Northern Ireland Act 1998. It has met on a regular basis since 1999. The Council meets in public and its decisions are formally recorded in minutes. The Council has key responsibilities in the area of working across the border on matters of mutual interest. These include economic and social development, education and learning, the environment, health and social care, and transport and infrastructure. The Council has a non-statutory role and its work is not legally enforceable. Ministers attend Council meetings in their ministerial capacities only.
The Environmental Protection Agency has designated the Corpus Christi Bay system as an estuary of national significance . More

1,000 miles long, the bay is one of the largest estuaries on the Texas coast. It is the second most productive bay on the Gulf Coast, after the Florida Bay, and is one of the most biologically diverse estuaries in the world. The bay is home to more than 1,000 species of plants and animals, including 12 endangered and threatened species. The bay is a popular venue for commercial fishing and recreational boating and wildlife watching.
 The bay is also the drinking water source for Corpus Christi and Port Aransas, and is a major source of drinking water for the region. The bay also supplies drinking water to more than 100,000 people in Victoria, Refugio, and San Patricio counties. Other uses of the bay include commercial and recreational fishing, agriculture and aquaculture, and recreation and tourism.
Source: EPA, Environmental Protection Agency, “Estuary of National Significance Designations,” [http://www.epa.gov/owow/nps/estuaries/natsign.html, accessed July 31, 2008].

The " Ode on Indolence " is one of five odes composed by English poet John Keats in the spring of 1819 . The others were " Ode

to Psyche ", " Ode  to a Nightingale ", " Ode on a Grecian Urn " and " Ode on Melancholy ". The title of the collection was "Odes", but the other four odes were published separately from "Ode on Indolence". The character of the Ode on Indolence differs from those of the others in that it contains only a single speaker, and is not addressed to any particular person or object of worship.  This is the only poem in which Keats uses the preposition "to" in any of his odes.   The opening line of the Ode on Indolence is "Oh! for a life of sensations rather than of thoughts!"  Keats wrote the Ode on Indolence at the time when he was at his most exuberant, and it is the only ode to be written in the middle of the day, and it is the most expansive in its imagery.  Keats wrote it in the summer of 1819, while he was staying with his brother George on the Isle of Wight, and it was published anonymously in the week following his death.  It was not printed until 1828, and it is the only one of the odes not to be dedicated to a particular person or object of worship. The Chapel of the Holy Angels and Archangels ( Spanish : Capilla de los Ángeles ) was finished in 1665 with Baroque altarpieces

by Alonso Berruguete and Juan Martínez Montañés . The chapel is located in the church of Santo Domingo el Real in Salamanca , Spain and is currently used for religious services.
The Capilla de los Ángeles was built in 1662 and was finished the following year. The architect was Juan Gómez de Mora, and the main altarpieces were made by the sculptors Alonso Berruguete and Juan Martínez Montañés, each responsible for two of the three altarpieces.
Berruguete's altarpiece, only one of which survives, shows the Archangels Michael and Gabriel . The figure of the Archangel Raphael is not present, as it was moved from the main altar to a nearby niche. The Saint Dominic figure in the central altarpiece is that of the founder of the Dominicans , Saint Dominic de Guzmán , portrayed wearing the traditional habit of the order. The sculpture of Saint Dominic is by Alonso Berruguete, and the two figures of the Archangels are by Juan Martínez Montañés. The architect Gómez de Mora employed the same Gothic style as he did for the whole of the church of Santo Domingo el Real.
In the extreme left of the main altarpiece is the figure of Saint Catherine of Alexandria , painted by Luis Martínez de Peralta. Saint Catherine of Alexandria is the female figure in the central altarpiece, and is depicted wearing a blue dress. The other figures are of Saint Peter , Saint Paul and Saint Thomas , also painted by Martínez de Peralta. The central figure in the right altarpiece is Saint Francis of Assisi , painted by Luis Martínez de Peralta. The other figures in the altarpiece are of Saint Anthony of Padua , Saint John the Evangelist and Saint Dominic , again painted by Martínez de Peralta.
The Capilla de los Ángeles is currently used for religious services, and has a capacity for up to 100 people. The Capilla de los Ángeles is also used to hold concerts, and is the venue for the Salamanca International Gregorian Festival. The chapel was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1941.
As of 2013, the Capilla de los Ángeles is the only chapel in the church of Santo Domingo el Real that has retained its original interior decoration.

The second commandment prohibits the use of God 's name in vain . Many ancient cultures believed that names were sacred ; some

claimed that a person was  bound to the  name given to him at birth  and that it was too sacred to be used lightly . This belief was incorporated into the  Decalogue  as a warning against  blasphemy : " Thou shalt not take  the  name of the  Lord  thy God in vain ; for the  Lord  will not hold him guiltless that taketh  his name  in vain " ( Exod . 20 : 7 ).
 God 's name and majesty were  central  to scripture ; it was common to  invoke  it in the  presence  of  enemies , even if the prayer  did  not include a request for help . The  Septuagint  rendered the commandment by substituting the  Greek  word  blasphēmō  for  shamar , since in  Greek  the two words are similar in form and sound .
 In  ancient  Hebrew , a person 's name was considered so sacred that it was often  written  with the initial letter of the  name  in  capital  letters . This practice is often seen in  ancient  manuscripts , particularly those of the  Torah . In  Judaism , the  sages  emulated this practice and  wrote  the  Name  of God with the initial letters of the word in capital letters : " YHWY " . This practice is known in  Judaism  as " tetragrammaton " , " four letters " , or " the  four  letters of  God 's  name ".

The final stage occurs when a massive star begins producing iron . Since iron nuclei are more tightly bound than any heavier nu

clide, they are not destroyed by fusion reactions. Moreover, the force of gravity is so strong that it eventually overcomes the outward pressure of these fusion reactions, causing the star to collapse. If the star has a mass of less than about eight solar masses, it collapses into a dense, hot sphere called a white dwarf , which is not quite as hot as the Sun, but only about 5,000C. The collapse of the star is so rapid that there is no time for the fusion process to continue. A white dwarf is about the size of Earth, but with a mass some hundred thousand times greater than that of our planet. Since so much mass is packed into such a small volume, the density is enormous. The interior of a white dwarf is about as dense as the nucleus of an atom. When the pressure within the white dwarf becomes great enough, the atoms collapse into an electron gas, with a density about one-millionth the density of water. The temperature of the electron gas is about 1 millionC.

The action was the first of two in this campaign in which lone British frigates were briefly overwhelmed by superior French for

ays. The first, the affair of the _St. George_, had been fought off the east coast of Ireland on the 8th of May, 1796, and the second took place off the Irish coast on the 16th of September, 1796. The frigate was the _Waterwitch_, of 38 guns, and the French force was a squadron of seven vessels, consisting of the 74-gun _Fougueux_, the 74-gun _Vengeur_, the 74-gun _Achille_, the 74-gun _Aigle_, the 74-gun _Indomptable_, and the 28-gun _Confiance_, with 4 bomb vessels and 2 gun boats. The action took place some 20 miles N.W. of Kinsale. Having been in sight of the enemy for some hours, the commander of the _Waterwitch_ decided upon the attack. This was delayed, however, by the breaking up of the fleet in a squall, and it was not until 6 a.m. on the 16th that the _Waterwitch_ was ready. At this time the enemy was in sight, and there was a brisk cannonade for half an hour. The French, however, were making all sail to the eastward, and at 7 a.m. the _Waterwitch_ began her chase. The French continued a little to the eastward until 11 a.m., then ran up the river Blackwater, and the _Waterwitch_ was obliged to fall off and stand to the westward. The enemy was now 10 miles off, and the _Waterwitch_ was unable to overhaul them. At 4 p.m. the French squadron disappeared from the view of the _Waterwitch_. The French lost one man killed and one wounded, and the British one man wounded. The French squadron made some 30 or 40 miles up the river Blackwater, and anchored in the bar of the river Shannon. The ships then separated, the _Fougueux_ and _Vengeur_ proceeding to the Shannon, the _Achille_ and _Aigle_ to the estuary of the river Lee, and the _Indomptable_ and _Confiance_ proceeding to Kinsale. The _Fougueux_ and _Vengeur_ anchored in the river Shannon, and the _Confiance_ and the bomb vessels anchored in the river Lee. The _Achille_ and _Aigle_ came up the river Lee and anchored in the bar of the river Lee. On the 17th the _Fougueux_ and _Vengeur_ came down the Shannon, and the _Achille_ down the Lee. The _Indomptable_ and _Confiance_ came down to Kinsale, and on the 19th the whole squadron weighed anchor, and proceeded to Cork.

It was the prevailing wisdom that the House of Lords could not amend money bills , since only the House of Commons had the righ

t to make or amend laws. The devolvement of that right was the grant of the power of taxation to the House of Commons during the 17th century. However, the Lords still had an important role: to scrutinise the Commons' work, and to speak for the people of the country as a whole, rather than just the Members of Parliament who sat in the Commons. As a result, the Lords had the power to reject money bills, but they did not have the power to amend them. In the 2000s, the Labour government claimed that the Lords had the power to amend money bills , and that the Lords should therefore be able to amend the Finance Bill, as this was a money bill . The Lords rejected this claim, and the matter even reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court decided that the Lords did indeed have the power to amend money bills, and the Lords did indeed have the power to amend the Finance Bill. On the 23rd of May 2011, the Lords did indeed amend the Finance Bill, and the bill was duly passed by the Commons and the Queen gave the Royal Assent.

WASP @-@ 13 was observed between February 11 and 15 in 2008 by the SOPHIE échelle spectrograph at the Haute @-@ Provence Observ

atoire (France). We obtained 8 spectra with a resolution of $R=~52,000$ covering the spectral range between 385 and 890 nm. The position of WASP @-@ 13 is near the edge of the field of view of SOPHIE. The radial velocities were measured by cross-correlating the spectra with a synthetic spectrum computed for a model star of spectral type F5V in order to reduce the impact of the stellar activity. We find that WASP @-@ 13 has a very low level of activity (a mean S $\sigma$ $=$ 0.4 $\pm$ 0.2 m s$^{-1}$) that is similar to that of stars in the middle of the activity sequence of F-dwarfs. The low level of activity of WASP @-@ 13, combined with its low mass (0.57 $\pm$ 0.02 M$_{\odot}$) and age (0.4 $\pm$ 0.1 Gyr), gives a high probability of life on its surface. We also find that WASP @-@ 13 has a low mass ratio (q $=$ 0.31 $\pm$ 0.08) and a high eccentricity (e $=$ 0.71 $\pm$ 0.02). The combination of these parameters give a good probability that WASP @-@ 13 is a pulsar. Additionally, we find that the line bisector span (BIS) of WASP @-@ 13 is very low ($<$ 3.5 $\times$ 10$^{-4}$) compared to solar-like stars. Harold Adams Innis ( / ˈɪnɪs / ; November 5 , 1894 – November 8 , 1952 ) was a Canadian professor of political economy at the U

of T and a prolific author of books on history and media of communication. He believed that the development of media was the defining feature of Western history and that these media had a general effect on human culture .
He was born in London, UK to Vaughan and Maud Ellen (née Lecacheur) Innis . His father was a shareholder in the London Naval Gun Factory and a director of the London and North Western Railway . His mother was the daughter of Canadian politician Robert Lecacheur . At the age of 22, he moved to Canada and settled in Winnipeg , where he worked for the Exchange Telegraph Company . At the end of World War I , he was hired by the Winnipeg Tribune . He graduated with a BA from the University of Manitoba in 1921. He was a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada . In 1930, he was elected to the American Philosophical Society , and in 1938 to the Royal Society of Arts . He was a member of the board of governors of the International Institute of Arts and Letters (1945–1951).
His first book was The Fur Trade in Canada (1923). In Canada's Problem Children (1936), Innis argued that the lack of social and economic mobility in Canada was due to the fact that the country's political, economic, and educational institutions were all controlled by a small, upper-class elite. In The Bias of Communication (1951), Innis outlined his theory of the bias of modern communication, arguing that the mass media were biased in favor of the business class and against the working class. In The Interpretation of Culture (1952), Innis argued that all cultures change over time, but that some changes are more important than others. He believed that the most important changes were those that occurred in the fields of communication and technology, because these changes had a major impact on the way people thought and behaved.
Innis's best known work is probably The Cod Fisheries: The History of an International Economy (1941). In this book, Innis argues that the cod fisheries were the most important international economy in the world during the Middle Ages. He believes that the development of the cod fisheries was an important factor in the development of Western civilization.
Innis was married to Ellen (née St. John) from 1920 until her death in 1955.
Innis died on November 8 , 1952 , at the age of 58 . His remains were cremated and his ashes were scattered over Lake Ontario in the Toronto Islands .

Thurgood Marshall (July 2, 1908 – January 24, 1993) was an American lawyer, civil rights activist, and the first African American to be on the United States Supreme Court. He was nominated by President John F. Kennedy to replace Justice William O. Douglas and served from 1967 to 1991.

The film ends with Tom and his daughter playing together in the village , as the villagers look on in awe.

2nd century AD to the 16th century. The name of the island, Eilean Bàn (white island), is thought to refer to the white sandstone outcrops of the peninsula. In 1999, the island was designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest. A number of archaeological sites can be seen on the island, including the remains of a 2nd century AD hut circle settlement, a 16th century tower house and the remains of a medieval chapel. A 19th century chapel ruins are also located on the island. The ruins of the chapel are the only remains of the parish church of Rodel which was destroyed by the Vikings in the 9th century. The Rodel chapel was built by the Clan Ranald in 1890. The island was reacquired by the National Trust for Scotland in 2013. The National Trust manages the island and the two other islands in the Sound of Harris. The islands were purchased by the Trust for the benefit of the public, with the intention of protecting them from development. The islands are accessible by ferry from Lochmaddy, South Uist, during the summer months. The Sound of Harris is a strait between the Isle of Lewis and the island of Harris. Ælfric of Abingdon ( Old English : Ælfrīc ; died 16 November 1005 ) , also known as Ælfric of Wessex , was a late 10th @-@ cent

ur y English author, scholar and priest. He was the first scholar in the English language to write in a serious manner on biblical subjects. He is one of the main figures in the development of Old English literature and the English language .
He was born in the village of Abbotsbury, Dorset, and educated at the monastery of Abingdon , Berkshire , where he became a monk and was ordained a priest . His presence at Abingdon was noted by the chronicler William of Malmesbury , who also notes that his works are preserved in Abingdon Abbey's library.
His writings, which are also preserved in that library, are considered to be the most important extant Anglo-Saxon works. The only other English texts of comparable quality are those of Wulstan , Archbishop of York , and Aelfric's own contemporary, Æthelweard of Winchester . They are also the oldest surviving texts in the English language, and they contain many of the earliest surviving examples of Old English , the Old English vernacular of Anglo-Saxon England .
The first book he is known to have written was on the sacrament of baptism . The earliest manuscripts of some of his works may date to the 990s, although they were not completed until the latter half of the 11th century ; others may be much later. His works have been dated from the 1000s to the 1100s, and he is sometimes called Ælfric of the 11th century, in order to distinguish him from Ælfric of Eynsham , the later 11th-century priest who was a contemporary of the papacy rather than the Anglo-Saxon monarchy . His works are written in Old English , though not always in the dialect of Wessex , in which he was educated.
The Old English scholar Robert M. Liuzza writes that Ælfric's works "represent an important turning point in the history of Old English literature" and that his works "set a new standard" for the vernacular literature of the period. They are often considered the earliest examples of Old English prose. His Latin works were not preserved in the Abingdon Abbey library, according to William of Malmesbury, and it has been suggested that Ælfric destroyed them in order to avoid the perceived threat to Christianity posed by the Norman Conquest .

The Pentwyn Link Road ( Welsh : Ffordd Gyswllt Pentwyn ) , which is also known as the North Pentwyn Link Road , runs from the P

entyrch Road in Llanishen to the A4232 road at the Pentyrch Road roundabout in Pentwyn , Cardiff, Wales . The road is approximately 2.5 kilometres (1.6 mi) in length and runs through the area of North Pentwyn , which is located in the north of the city. The road is mainly built on greenfield land and is part of the Cardiff Western Expansion Scheme .
The road was constructed in two phases, the first of which opened in May 2005 and saw the road laid between the Pentyrch Road and the A4232. The second phase opened in 2007 and saw the road extended to the area of Tremorfa . The road was constructed with a single lane in each direction and a 20 mph (32 km/h) speed limit .
The road was constructed in order to alleviate traffic congestion in the area of North Pentwyn and provide a link between the Pentyrch Road and the A4232. The road was constructed in order to coincide with the construction of the North Pentwyn housing development .
In 2007, the Welsh Assembly Government confirmed that the Pentwyn Link Road would be constructed at the same time as the A4232 Cardiff Eastern Relief Road .

trans retinoic acid ( ATRA ) . ATRA has no antileukemic effect in AML patients in the absence of retinoic acid receptors ( RARs ) . ATRA binds to RARs and activates them , which leads to the induction of differentiation and cell death of AML cells .
 ATRA also enhances the antileukemic activity of the antibiotic arsenic trioxide ( As2O3 ) , which downregulates the expression of the AML -specific promyelocytic leukemia protein ( PML ) . PML translocates to the nucleus where it binds with retinoic acid responsive elements ( RAREs ) and inhibits the expression of genes that are responsible for leukemia . As2O3 causes the translocation of PML into the cytosol where it combines with the protein PML - nuclear bodies ( PML - NBs ) to form PML - NBs , which are usually located in the nucleus . The translocation of PML to the cytosol decreases the expression of genes responsible for leukemia and leads to the differentiation of AML cells .
 When ATRA is combined with arsenic trioxide , the activity of ATRA is increased because of the downregulation of PML , which is required for the differentiation of AML cells and the inhibition of gene expression . This combination also increases the sensitivity of AML cells to the drug .

On 23 May 2017, following the election of the Conservative Party to a minority government with 326 seats in the House of Commons , party leader Theresa May made a statement to the House of Commons regarding the formation of a new government, and her intention to seek the approval of the Queen to form her new government on 26 May . According to the convention that no government should seek to rely exclusively on a single party's support in the House of Commons, May sought to initiate a period of "confidence and supply" to enable her government to continue to function.
It was reported on 24 May that May's coalition with the Democratic Unionist Party ( DUP ) would be supported by a letter signed by the DUP leader Arlene Foster , and by four other DUP MPs . The DUP has no MPs in the House of Lords . The letter was later amended, and also signed by the DUP's Nigel Dodds . The DUP has 10 seats in the House of Commons .
In a televised statement on 24 May , May said that the DUP had agreed to provide support on certain individual matters of confidence and supply , although she did not provide further details. At the same time, she announced that the DUP would not be appointed to any government ministry , and would have no formal role in government.

The Good Friday Agreement was formally endorsed by referendums in both parts of Ireland , which became known as the Good Friday Agreement .
In Northern Ireland , the agreement was endorsed by 71.1% of the electorate who voted in the referendum on 22 May 1998 ; in the Republic of Ireland , 94.4% voted in favour of the agreement in the referendum on 18 May .
The Agreement established the Northern Ireland Assembly and the Northern Ireland Executive in Northern Ireland , ending the direct rule of the United Kingdom over Northern Ireland .
In the Republic of Ireland , it secured the establishment of a new Irish language Act and was the subject of Republic of Ireland Acts 1998 and 2003 , which established the Irish Language Act 2003 and the Irish Language ( Civil Service ) Act 2003 .
The Agreement also provided for a new British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference , which has the responsibility for considering and resolving disputes between the United Kingdom and Ireland .
In Northern Ireland , the Agreement established a new political structure for Northern Ireland , consisting of three pillars , which are:
The political pillar consists of a Northern Ireland Assembly and a Northern Ireland Executive , both elected by the people of Northern Ireland .
The institutional pillar consists of bodies in the areas of policing and criminal justice , human rights , and public administration .
The social and economic pillar consists of bodies in the areas of education , culture , inward investment , and economic development .

The fossils of these animals were decayed beyond recognition , except for the occasional piece of bone or tooth. The bones had been eroded by the elements and the water, and had been replaced by the minerals found in the soil. As a result , the remains could not be identified with confidence , and it was not until the early 1900s that a new technique was discovered that could identify the remains.
The technique was called chemical etching , and it involved applying a solution to the bones that would dissolve away the minerals and leave the original bone behind. The technique was so effective that it allowed scientists to identify the remains of dinosaurs with certainty for the first time, and it has since been used to identify the remains of other prehistoric animals as well.
The discovery of chemical etching as a way to identify prehistoric fossils was a major breakthrough in paleontology. It allowed scientists to identify animals that had been lost for millions of years, and it has since been used to study the evolution of life on Earth. Chemical etching is now a standard part of the study of prehistoric fossils, and it has helped to fill in the gaps in our knowledge of prehistory.

In an early review in the 1831 Westminster Review , J. Fox praises the depiction of women within the whole of Poems , Chiefly L

yrical , as well as in the individual poems.  He finds particular cause to celebrate the depiction of female characters in 'The Eve of St. Agnes' in comparison to other depictions of women in poetry.  In 'St. Agnes' Eve', the poet 'relieves the sex from the tyranny of sketchy and conventional beauty' (p. 140) by refusing to draw his female characters and instead focusing on their inner moral and psychological states.  The poem's characters therefore 'combine all the charms of human nature, whatever its sex' (p. 140). Fox also praises Keats's depiction of women in 'La Belle Dame sans Merci' and 'The Eve of St. Agnes' as depicting their 'true and natural character' in contrast to the more superficial depictions of women in other literary works.
Emily Lorraine de Montluzin , 'Keats and the Romantic Critique of the Feminine', in The New Keats: Essays from the Keats-Shelley House Centenary Conference , ed. by Rachel Austen and Deidre Lynch (New York: Fordham University Press, 2009), p. 125.
Mary Jacobus , Reading Woman: Essays in Feminist Criticism (New York: Columbia University Press, 1986), pp. 157-66.

In Mexico , the diamond stingray is one of the most important components of Pacific artisanal shark and ray fisheries , compris

ing about 20% of annual landings . The majority of these rays are caught by non-professional fishermen who use hook and line to catch the rays . A few individuals also use gillnets . The species is predominantly found in the Gulf of California and the Gulf of Tehuantepec (Mexico) . The average weight of the stingray is 20 to 40 kg , with a maximum weight of 50 kg , and a length of 1 . 7 m . The stingray is an important part of the diet in the Mexican Pacific and is consumed , both raw and cooked . The flesh is considered delicious and is sold in markets and restaurants throughout the Mexican Pacific . The stingray is also a popular subject of local folk art products . The stingray is considered by many as a delicacy , and is often eaten in large quantities , especially during religious festivals . The stingray is also used for medicinal purposes in certain areas . The stingray is a target of overfishing . As a consequence , the sustainability of the species is questioned . The international trade in the stingray is regulated by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) , which is a multilateral treaty aimed at protecting the most endangered species of wild fauna and flora . The species is listed in Appendix II of the CITES regulations , which means it is not endangered , but requires regulation to avoid overexploitation . Possibly the most pervasive influence on Walpole was Walter Scott , whose romanticism is reflected in much of the later writer

s  work. Scott  s influence on Walpole  s poetry is undeniable. The first and last lines of his poetry, for example, are almost identical. He even attempts to recreate in his works the same atmosphere of the medieval Scottish barons who fought for the crown.  (Lavin, 171)
Consider the following lines from Walpole  s  poem  William and Margaret :
But, as he thought on Margaret, he knew
The only way to her was through the wood
And there before him lay an opening,
Sweeping the path, the rest shut out from view.
He could not think, he could not hesitate,
But, taking his horse, he set him at the gate.
Tho  the path was rough he soon was through,
And scarce had reached the bottom of the wood
When he heard a voice, which, full of plaint
And trouble, called,  Follow me!  . . . 
But Margaret was gone, and William could not see;
He knew not how to find the path again,
Nor how to guide his horse to Margaret. (Hollander, 546)
These lines describe a situation which is very reminiscent of the opening of Sir Walter Scott s  poem  Marmion.  William, like Marmion, decides to go through the wood in search of his beloved, Margaret. He had almost reached the bottom of the wood, but when he hears her voice he loses his way. If we were to compare the two poems in more detail, Walpole  s  poem becomes even more striking. William and Margaret is similar to Marmion in that both poems are about a man who is too impetuous to follow the advice of an old friend. William and Margaret stops short at the point when Marmion reaches the chapel of St. Michael. In Marmion, the old friend  s  advice is most important because it contains an important lesson. The first stanza of Marmion tells us that “Sir William Marmion, the pride of his clan, / Had, as the bard sings, been a knight renowned, / But for the love of a woman  s  light word / He left his home, and broke the  bond of kindred. “ (Hollander, 546) The poem sets up a very strong image of the knight, William Marmion, as a hero. He is the perfect example of a noble and chivalrous man. This is the man whom the old friend, Sir Richard, advises to stay home and marry “a fair and blushing maiden. “ (Hollander, 547) But Marmion is impetuous, and he cannot listen to his friend. Instead, he goes through the wood, and he loses his way. He can  t find his way back home, and he must suffer for his impetuousness and rashness. So, as Marmion reaches the chapel of St. Michael, he is on the verge of death. In William and Margaret, William suffers for his impetuousness, but he is not, as Marmion was, on the verge of death. Walpole  s  poem is more sentimental than Scott  s. In Marmion, we are less concerned with the fate of the knight, but rather with the fate of his beloved, Margaret, and his friend, Sir Richard, who is waiting outside the chapel of St. Michael. Scott himself comments on this in the introduction to Marmion. “The true theme of the poem, which has been too much overlooked, is the fate of Margaret.  “ (Hollander, 545) In William and Margaret, Walpole  s  main concern is with the fate of William and Margaret. Margaret is the heroine, and she is the one who will be punished for her rashness. In the beginning of Walpole  s  poem, Margaret is speaking to William, and she is saying that he must not go through the wood, that it is too dangerous, but he ignores her. The same thing happens in Marmion. Margaret tells Marmion that he should not go through the wood, but he does not listen to her. In the end, both of them are punished for their impetuousness. When Margaret loses her way in the wood, she is rescued by a knight, and they ride together towards Sir Richard. But Margaret is punished for her impetuousness in a very different way. She is forced to stay in the chapel of St. Michael, and she must wait for Marmion to come. She is trapped in the chapel, and she is forced to face her punishment. She must face the consequences of her impetuousness. Walpole  s  poem is more sentimental than Marmion. He leaves out the part about the punishment, but he keeps the part about the impetuousness. In the end, both William and Marmion are punished for their impetuousness. Walpole

Hurricane Lorenzo was a rapidly developing tropical cyclone that struck the Mexican state of Veracruz in late September 2007 .

Lorenzo was the first major hurricane of the Eastern Pacific hurricane season of 2007 and the first major hurricane in the Atlantic basin since Hurricane Dean struck the Caribbean in August. Lorenzo was the strongest hurricane on record in the eastern Atlantic basin south of the equator. It was also the strongest Hurricane to strike Mexico south of the Tampico-Tuxpan line. Lorenzo passed as close as 40 miles (64 km) to Playa del Carmen , Quintana Roo and the closest to the Yucatan Peninsula making landfall to the west of the city of Veracruz. In Veracruz, Lorenzo left a trail of destruction with a storm surge of 6 feet (1.8 m) and wind gusts of up to 100 mph (130 mph). Lorenzo caused $1 billion in damage and 27 fatalities. The United States Catechism for Adults devotes a section to in vitro fertilization , stem @-@ cell research and cloning in its

175 pages. But readers looking for a similar treatment of the Catechism’s teaching on the subject of human cloning will be disappointed. The text of the catechism, which is more than 3,000 pages long, and the authors of the Catechism for Adults have resisted calls by Church leaders to include the teaching on cloning in their volume.
It would be hard to blame the Catechism committee for ignoring human cloning. The teaching on human cloning is a minor issue in the Catechism when compared to more serious doctrinal questions, such as the relation of Mary to the Incarnation or the Six Days of Creation. What makes it so easy to ignore the issue is the fact that the International Theological Commission has not issued a formal statement on cloning. The ITC is a committee of cardinals, archbishops, and bishops appointed by the pope to study and issue authoritative statements on doctrinal questions. Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, the pope’s chief doctrinal advisor, has made clear that human cloning, which involves the destruction of human embryos for the purpose of creating a human clone, is gravely contrary to the teachings of the Church.
As the Institute for Human Ecology’s Daniel Maguire has pointed out, there is plenty of material for the Catechism committee to draw upon in its treatment of cloning. The Church has repeatedly condemned the destruction of human embryos, so there is no problem finding sources from which to condemn human cloning. The Catechism of the Catholic Church devotes several paragraphs to the destruction of embryos for research, and several paragraphs to the destruction of embryos for the purpose of therapeutic abortion. There is no good reason not to treat the destruction of embryos for the purpose of human cloning as gravely sinful.
The Catechism committee has produced a very useful volume. It is a thorough treatment of the Catholic faith. It would be beneficial if the committee also tackled the question of human cloning.

Fez was first announced in July 2007 on The Independent Gaming Source . A trailer released in October 2007 convinced Jason DeGr

asse to write a preview of Fez , which was published on 9 November 2007. The preview was very positive and praised the game, and in February 2008 Fez was named a "Hot Game To Watch" by GameSpot . In June 2008 Fez was officially announced on the Xbox Live Marketplace and a demo version was released the following day (June 17). It was later revealed that it was the first game to be released on the Xbox Live Indie Games service. Fez was released on 21 July 2008. The game is available for download from the Xbox Live Indie Games service. A Facebook game of the same name was released on 18 November 2008. The game's Facebook page has since been removed. Fez was released in North America on Xbox 360 on 7 May 2012, and in Europe on 10 May 2012.
Fez is about a 2D world seen from a top-down perspective, which is transformed into a 3D world by rotating the player's view. In the real world, it appears that the game's protagonist, the blue cube Fez, has fallen into a void and is surrounded by four walls. Fez's head, however, is covered with a green gem which gives him the power to rotate his environment around himself; when he rotates the world, he changes his perspective from a 2D world to a three-dimensional one. By rotating the world, Fez is able to reach different areas of the world by moving through the walls. The game world is made up of "tiles"; by rotating the world, the player can "jump" from tile to tile to move through the world. The game is based on an original idea by Phil Fish, who believed that if the game world were rotated and the player could "jump" from tile to tile, it would make a perfect game.
The game world is filled with puzzles, in which the player must manipulate the environment in order to progress. The player must also collect 20 "fez coins" in each level, which serve as health in the game; when the player is killed, they respawn at the same level they were at when they died, but with less health. The game offers two difficulty levels: Normal and Hard. Normal is the default mode, where the player must collect all the fez coins to proceed to the next level, and Hard makes the game more difficult by giving the player less health, making it harder to complete the levels. The game also features a "troubleshooting" mode, which allows the player to rotate the world without the use of the gem.
The game features a soundtrack by Disasterpeace , and the soundtrack for Fez won the "Best Music" award at the Independent Games Festival in 2012. A soundtrack for Fez was released digitally on 16 May 2012.
Fez was well received by critics. GameRankings and Metacritic gave it a score of 88.67% and 88/100 respectively, indicating "generally favourable reviews".
IGN gave it 9.0 out of 10, calling it "The game 2D platformers have always wanted to be, but never could be." The Telegraph rated it 8 out of 10, saying that "The most interesting thing about Fez is how utterly unique it is." 1UP.com gave it 9 out of 10, calling it "the best 2.5D game you'll ever experience."
Fez has sold 100,000 copies, with a total of over 1 million downloads. This was enough to get it on the list of the top 20 fastest selling Xbox Live Indie Games of all time, with a $100,000 profit. It was the second fastest selling game on the Xbox Live Indie Games service, behind Shadow Complex . A sequel, Fez 2 , was released on 10 July 2013.

This definition is now used by the IAU to distinguish a dwarf planet from a planet. The IAU acknowledges that there are no universally accepted criteria to distinguish planets from dwarf planets, and that while there are some candidates for planets that may not be dwarf planets, there are no known dwarf planets that may not be planets. A successful generalist predator , the cougar will eat any animal it can catch , from insects to large ungulates ( over 500 kg

1100 lb 7 1 t ). It is the largest terrestrial cat in the Americas and the third largest in the world after the tiger and the jaguar . Though cats in general are opportunistic hunters , the cougar is an especially flexible predator that can kill and eat prey as large as 50 percent of its body mass , or a 200 lb 91 kg 2 2 t animal , provided it is young and healthy . The cougar is a generalist hunter , taking a wide variety of prey , such as deer , wild pigs , wild turkey , and other small mammals and birds . It will attack large animals such as elk and bison , but it will not attack animals larger than itself . Its diet varies geographically , with the main prey species in the Southeastern United States being white tail deer , but in other areas , such as coastal regions of California , grazing animals such as elk are preferred . The cougar has a reputation for being a solitary animal , but it is actually a social animal that occasionally hunts in groups or in pairs . It spends most of its time alone , however , and it is not uncommon for a male cougar to have more than one female as a mate at a time . A dominant male will drive away a subordinate male from a territory . They have been known to live in small family groups for several months , with the dominant male and female and their dependent offspring . It is not uncommon for a cougar to be killed by another cougar , especially by a dominant male . A female could lose her offspring to a dominant male , and a male could lose his territory to a larger more dominant male . Males also lose their territories when they become old and infirm , and a female then takes over . A female will also give birth to a litter of cubs , usually 2 to 4 , and raise them for a few years before the young disperse to find their own places in the ecosystem . Although cougars have been hunted to the point where they are considered rare , they are still common in many parts of the United States , and they are not endangered . Isabella Mayson was born on 14 March 1836 in Marylebone , London . She was the eldest of three daughters to Benjamin Mayson , a

hairdresser , and his wife, Annis , née Knight . Isabella was baptised on 20 March 1836 in St Marylebone , Marylebone , London . She was the second child , after Benjamin , to be born to Benjamin and Annis . She had a brother , James , and a sister , Mary Ann , who died within a few months of her birth . Isabella was living with her parents in Marylebone , London , at the time of the 1841 census , where she was described as an unmarried 5 year old . Benjamin was a hairdresser . On 30 March 1844 , at St Marylebone , Isabella married Thomas Mawer , a 27 year old hairdresser , who was living with his parents , Mary and Robert Mawer , a stationer , at 26 Gower Street , Bloomsbury , London . The witnesses were her mother , Annis , and Thomas' sister , Mary Ann Mawer . Thomas' father , Robert Mawer , died in 1844 , and on 4 December 1851 , at St Marylebone , Isabella married Thomas' brother , John Mawer , a 41 year old corn merchant , who was living with his wife, Sarah , née Penn , at 14 Abbey Terrace , Oxford Street , Marylebone , London . The witnesses were her sister , Mary Ann , and John's brother , Robert Mawer . Isabella was living in Marylebone at the time of the 1851 census , where she was described as a housekeeper . By this time her son , Benjamin , and her daughter , Sarah , were born . Isabella was living with her sister , Mary Ann Knight , at 22 Seymour Place , Marylebone , London , at the time of the 1871 census . She was described as a widow and a dressmaker . She was buried at St Thomas the Martyr , Marylebone , London , on 22 November 1877 .
